Global Optimality for Constrained Exploration
via Penalty Regularization

Florian Wolf  22footnotemark: 2 ††thanks: Corresponding author: fwolf@caltech.edu    Ilyas Fatkhullin33footnotemark: 3    Niao He33footnotemark: 3    22footnotemark: 2   California Institute of Technology 33footnotemark: 3   ETH Zürich & ETH AI Center
Abstract

Efficient exploration is a central problem in reinforcement learning and is often formalized as maximizing the entropy of the state-action occupancy measure. While unconstrained maximum-entropy exploration is relatively well understood, real-world exploration is often constrained by safety, resource, or imitation requirements. This constrained setting is particularly challenging because entropy maximization lacks additive structure, rendering Bellman-equation-based methods inapplicable. Moreover, scalable approaches require policy parameterization, inducing non-convexity in both the objective and the constraints. To our knowledge, the only prior model-free policy-gradient approach for this setting under general policy parameterization is due to Ying et al. 2025 [135]. Unfortunately, their guarantees are limited to weak regret and ergodic averages, which do not imply that the final output is a single deployable policy that is near-optimal and nearly feasible. In this work we take a different approach to this problem, and propose Policy Gradient Penalty (PGP) method, a single-loop policy-space method that enforces general convex occupancy-measure constraints via quadratic-penalty regularization. PGP constructs pseudo-rewards that yield gradient estimates of the penalized objective, subsequently exploiting the classical Policy Gradient Theorem. We further establish the regularity of the penalized objective, providing the smoothness properties needed to justify the convergence of PGP. Leveraging hidden convexity and strong duality, we then establish global last-iterate convergence guarantees, attaining an ε{\varepsilon}-optimal constrained entropy value with ε{\varepsilon}-bounded constraint violation despite policy-induced non-convexity. We validate PGP through ablations on a grid-world benchmark and further demonstrate scalability on two challenging continuous-control tasks.11 1 Code available under: https://github.com/Flo-Wo/penalty-based-constrained-exploration.

1 Introduction

Efficient exploration is a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in the absence of an external reward signal, where the goal is to acquire broad and informative coverage of the environment rather than optimize task-specific returns. A principled line of work formulates pure exploration as maximizing the entropy of the state-action occupancy measure induced by a policy, encouraging diverse visitation of the environment [50]. This viewpoint has led to substantial progress in entropy-based exploration, with both theoretical and practical advances [90, 111].

In realistic systems, however, exploration is inherently constrained not only by safety limits and resource budgets, but crucially by imitation requirements, where policies must remain close to a given prior or expert behavior while still exploring novel regions of the state-action space [41]. Despite their importance, existing approaches to constrained entropy-based exploration are largely heuristic [128, 112]. The model-based approaches of Agarwal et al. [2], Bai et al. [9] operate with explicit representations of the state-action occupancy measure, which limits their applicability in large-scale or continuous settings where function approximation is required. In contrast, Ying et al. [135] provide only ergodic and weak-regret guarantees under restrictive assumptions.

A natural way to model safety, cost, and imitation requirements is to express them as convex constraints on the state-action occupancy measure, yielding a unified and expressive formulation for both finite- and infinite-horizon Markov decision processes. Achieving scalability, however, necessitates policy parameterization, which obscures this convex structure and eliminates the additive Bellman structure underlying standard dynamic-programming and actor-critic methods. Together with enforcing constraints under stochastic, truncated trajectory sampling with biased gradients, this leads to highly challenging optimization problems.

Contributions.

We develop a penalty framework for constrained maximum-entropy exploration that operates directly in policy space while retaining the hidden-convex structure of occupancy-measure optimization.22 2 In Appendix 0.D, we further extend our framework beyond RL to constrained hidden-convex optimization problems with possibly non-smooth objectives and constraints, which could be of independent interest. Our contributions are:

  1. (C1)

    We introduce PGP, a single-loop, primal-only Policy Gradient Penalty method for constrained maximum-entropy exploration that operates directly in policy space and enforces non-convex constraints via a quadratic penalty. By explicitly utilizing the RL structure of the problem, we construct pseudo-rewards, enabling single batch penalty gradient estimation.

  2. (C2)

    We prove global, non-asymptotic last-iterate convergence of PGP under biased stochastic gradients, despite the non-convexity induced by policy parametrization. The analysis quantifies the smoothness of the penalty formulation, a key property needed to establish global convergence, and provides a principled choice of the penalty regularization parameter.

  3. (C3)

    In the finite-MDP setting covered by our theory, we validate PGP on a grid world, demonstrating robustness to penalty tuning and gradient noise and providing practical guidance for choosing the penalty parameter β\beta. Beyond our theory, continuous state-action experiments demonstrate scalability and stable late-iterate feasibility.

2 Related Work

Entropy Maximization.

Maximizing the entropy of the state-action occupancy measure was introduced by Hazan et al. [50] as a principled formulation of reward-free exploration. Subsequent work has focused on improving computational efficiency and practical performance, including non-parametric entropy estimation [89, 90], representation learning [107, 132], and successor-based approaches [75, 76]. On the theoretical side, Tiapkin et al. [111] established fast convergence rates for maximum-entropy exploration, while Zamboni et al. [138], Zamboni et al. [139] extended entropy-based exploration to partially observable Markov decision processes (MDPs). These works focus almost exclusively on the unconstrained setting. While they exploit the convex structure of the entropy objective in the occupancy-measure space, they do not address constraints and therefore cannot guarantee feasibility in safety- or resource-constrained environments.

Constrained Entropy-Based Exploration.

Several recent works have studied constrained entropy maximization empirically. Yang and Spaan [128] propose constrained entropy maximization for safe, task-agnostic exploration, and Tiboni et al. [112] apply entropy maximization under performance chance constraints to domain randomization for sim-to-real transfer in robotics. Related ideas appear in transfer and imitation settings [16, 129, 59], observer gain tuning [60, 80] and system identification under performance constraints [121, 149]. However, these methods are heuristic in nature and do not provide (global) convergence guarantees, even in tabular settings.

More broadly, constrained and safe RL has been extensively studied under the Constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) formulation [4], for instance, using primal-dual methods [37, 42, 133, 77, 119, 48, 36, 10, 38, 70, 84, 39], primal-only approaches [1, 24, 27, 130, 125, 116, 97, 21], and in Bayesian settings [5, 120, 6].

Convex Reinforcement Learning.

Unconstrained convex, or general-utility, RL generalizes classical RL by allowing the objective to be a convex functional of the state-action occupancy measure, instead of standard additive rewards [137]. In the unconstrained setting, Zhang et al. [144] establish global convergence guarantees in tabular MDPs, with subsequent extensions to function approximation and variance reduction [146, 11, 106], as well as to large-scale problems [51, 12]. Finite-trial formulations [91] have also been studied [92, 93]. Related directions include multi-agent convex RL [134], a mean-field perspective [47], and extensions to risk-sensitive MDPs [122], submodular objectives [100, 34], and robust convex RL [23]. Online variants of unconstrained convex RL have been investigated in [86, 82, 87, 13]. Closely related in spirit, Kalogiannis et al. [58] study policy gradient convergence in imperfect-information extensive-form games. In the optimization literature, Fatkhullin et al. [44] analyze algorithms for unconstrained stochastic optimization problems under hidden convexity and Fatkhullin et al. [45] develop algorithms for hidden convex constrained problems. We refer to Appendix 0.A for additional related work and a detailed technical comparison of our contributions to the two most closely related works, Zhang et al. [144] and Fatkhullin et al. [44].

In contrast, significantly fewer works address convex RL under complex (e.g., safety or imitation) constraints. Agarwal et al. [2] study constrained convex MDPs (CCMDPs) using a model-based approach over the occupancy-measure space with count-based approximations and direct policy parametrization, relying on a strong form of Slater’s condition. Bai et al. [9] relax this requirement to the classical Slater condition and propose a Kullback Leibler (KL) regularized primal-dual algorithm, still operating in a model-based occupancy-measure formulation. More recently, [135] is the first work to study CCMDPs under a general softmax policy parametrization using a policy-gradient approach in policy parameter space. However, the obtained guarantees are limited to weak regret and ergodic averages, i.e., 1N​∑k=1NF1​(θ(k))−F⋆≤ε\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}F_{1}(\theta^{(k)})-F^{\star}\leq\varepsilon and [1N​∑k=1NF2​(θ(k))]+≤ε\bigl[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}F_{2}(\theta^{(k)})\bigr]_{+}\leq\varepsilon, see for example the discussion in [88]. Such guarantees permit cancellations in constraint violations and, moreover, are not operational in practice: averaging or sampling from iterates in parameter space is generally ill-defined for policy networks. Relatedly, Zhang et al. [142] study convex constrained MDPs in an offline, model-based setting using primal-dual methods under different assumptions. Overall, existing approaches to constrained convex RL suffer from at least one of the following limitations: they rely on model-based or count-based formulations that do not scale beyond small discrete state-action spaces; they require (forms of) Slater’s condition which might fail to hold in practice; and they provide only ergodic guarantees, precluding at-any-time convergence of the last iterate.

More generally, it was observed for constrained MDPs [125, 54] that primal-only methods can be preferable in practice, due to fewer hyperparameters, simpler implementations, and faster convergence resulting from the absence of delayed dual updates.

3 Preliminaries

Notation.

For a finite set AA, we denote with |A|\lvert A\rvert the cardinality and with Δ⁡(A)\Delta(A) the (|A|−1)(\lvert A\rvert-1)-dimensional simplex, i.e. the space of probability distributions over AA. If not stated differently, ∥⋅∥\lVert\,\cdot\,{}\rVert denotes the standard ℓ2\ell^{2}-norm for vectors and the spectral norm for matrices, and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\,\cdot\,{},\,\cdot\,{}\rangle is the Euclidean inner product. A differentiable function F:Θ→ℝF:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}} is LL-smooth if the gradient is LL-Lipschitz continuous, L∈ℝ≥0L\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}. For an integer k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} define the set [k]≔{1,…,k}[k]\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,k\}. A notation 𝒪⁡(⋅){\OOSym\!\left(\,\cdot\,{}\right)} captures all dependencies except for the accuracy ε{\varepsilon} and 𝒪~⁡(⋅){\OOTildeSym\!\left(\,\cdot\,{}\right)} hides logarithmic terms in 1/ε\nicefrac{{1}}{{{\varepsilon}}}.

Markov Decision Process (MDP).

A discrete-time infinite-horizon discounted Markov Decision Process is a tuple 𝕄≔(𝒮,𝒜,r,ℙ,γ,μ0){\mathbb{M}}\coloneqq({\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{A}},r,{\mathbb{P}},\gamma,\mu_{0}), where 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} and 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} are finite sets of states and actions, respectively. At a discrete timestep t∈ℕ0t\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}, being in state st∈𝒮{s}_{t}\in{\mathcal{S}} taking an action at∈𝒜{a}_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}} yields a reward rt=r⁡(st,at)r_{t}=r({s}_{t},{a}_{t}), according to the reward function r:𝒮×𝒜→[−rmax,rmax]r:{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to[-r_{\max},r_{\max}], and a new state st+1∼ℙ(⋅|st,at){s}_{t+1}\sim{\mathbb{P}}(\,\cdot\,{}|{s}_{t},{a}_{t}) according to the transition probability kernel ℙ:𝒮×𝒜→Δ⁡(𝒮){\mathbb{P}}:{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to\Delta({\mathcal{S}}). rmax>0r_{\max}>0 gives an upper and lower bound on the reward. We define the value function of a trajectory τ≔(st,at)t∈ℕ0\tau\coloneqq({s}_{t},{a}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}} as the cumulative discounted reward V⁡(τ)≔(1−γ)⋅∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at),V(\tau)\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\cdot\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r({s}_{t},{a}_{t}), where μ0\mu_{0} denotes the initial state distribution, i.e. s0∼μ0{s}_{0}\sim\mu_{0}, and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) is the so-called discount factor. A mapping π:𝒮→Δ⁡(𝒜)\pi:{\mathcal{S}}\to\Delta({\mathcal{A}}) is called a (stationary) policy, and Π\Pi denotes set of all stationary policies. Combined with the initial distribution μ0\mu_{0}, it induces a probability measure over finite-length trajectories τ=(st,at)t=0T−1\tau=({s}_{t},{a}_{t})_{t=0}^{T-1} by sampling at∼π(⋅|st){a}_{t}\sim\pi(\,\cdot\,{}|{s}_{t}) at each timestep t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T, T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, i.e. p⁡(τ)≔μ0​(s0)​π​(a0|s0)⋅∏t=1T−1ℙ⁡(st|st−1,at−1)​π​(at|st)p(\tau)\coloneqq\mu_{0}({s}_{0})\pi({a}_{0}|{s}_{0})\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}{\mathbb{P}}({s}_{t}|{s}_{t-1},{a}_{t-1})\pi({a}_{t}|{s}_{t}).

Policy Parametrization.

Throughout this work, we will assume the common softmax policy parameterization

πθ​(a|s)≔exp⁡(ψ⁡(s,a,θ))∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(ψ⁡(s,a′,θ)),\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}({a}|{s})\coloneqq\frac{\exp(\psi({s},{a};\theta))}{\sum_{{a}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\exp(\psi({s},{a}^{\prime};\theta))},

where θ∈Θ⊂ℝp\theta\in\Theta\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, s∈𝒮{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}, a∈𝒜{a}\in{\mathcal{A}}, and a smooth function ψ:𝒮×𝒜×Θ→ℝ\psi:{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\times\Theta\to{\mathbb{R}}.

State-action Occupancy Measure (OM).

For any policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, we define the (state-action) occupancy measure λπθ:𝒮×𝒜→[0,1]\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}:{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to[0,1] as

λπθ​(s,a)≔(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​ℙμ0,πθ​(st=s,at=a),\displaystyle\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a})\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}{\mathbb{P}}_{\mu_{0},\pi_{\theta}}({s}_{t}={s},{a}_{t}={a}),

where ℙμ0,πθ{\mathbb{P}}_{\mu_{0},\pi_{\theta}} denotes the probability distribution of the Markov chain (st,at)t∈ℕ({s}_{t},{a}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{N}}} induced by the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and the initial state distribution μ0\mu_{0} under the transition probability kernel ℙ{\mathbb{P}}. We denote by Λ≔{λπ:π∈Π}\Lambda\coloneqq\{\lambda^{\pi}\;:\;\pi\in\Pi\} the set of all state-action occupancy measures induced by the stationary policies Π\Pi. Since |𝒮|,|𝒜|<∞\lvert{\mathcal{S}}\rvert,\lvert{\mathcal{A}}\rvert<\infty, we will interpret a λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda as an element of [0,1]|𝒮|×|𝒜|[0,1]^{\lvert{\mathcal{S}}\rvert\times\lvert{\mathcal{A}}\rvert}. For a parametrized policy, we will use the notations λ⁡(θ)\lambda(\theta) and λπθ\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}} interchangeably. Intuitively, since the OM captures the state-action visitation frequencies induced by a policy, it provides a principled foundation for defining exploration as maximizing the entropy of the induced state-action distribution.

4 Problem Formulation

For a convex, LL-smooth constraint ℛ:Λ→ℝ{\mathcal{R}}:\Lambda\to{\mathbb{R}} formulated in the state-action-occupancy measure, we formulate the following constrained-max-entropy problem:

maxθ∈Θ⁡F1​(θ)≔ℋ⁡(λπθ)=−𝔼(s,a)∼λπθ​[log⁡λπθ​(s,a)]​s.t.F2​(θ)≔ℛ⁡(λπθ)≤0.\displaystyle\max_{\theta\in\Theta}F_{1}(\theta)\coloneqq{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})=-{\mathbb{E}}_{({s},{a})\sim\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}}\!\left[\log\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a})\right]\;\;\mathrm{s.t.}\;\;F_{2}(\theta)\coloneqq{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})\leq 0. (CME)

We assume only that there exists a stationary policy πfeas∈Π\pi_{\rm feas}\in\Pi satisfying ℛ⁡(λπfeas)≤0{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\rm feas}})\leq 0. Since Λ\Lambda is a compact polytope in a finite MDP, and ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and ℛ{\mathcal{R}} are continuous, the corresponding problem over all stationary policies admits an optimizer π∗∈Π\pi^{*}\in\Pi. We denote its value by ℋ∗≔ℋ⁡(λπ∗){\mathcal{H}}^{*}\coloneqq{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda^{\pi^{*}}) and set F∗≔ℋ∗{F^{*}}\coloneqq{\mathcal{H}}^{*}. We call θ^∈Θ{\hat{\theta}}\in\Theta an (ε,ε)({\varepsilon},{\varepsilon})-optimal solution if |𝔼⁡[F1​(θ^)−F∗]|≤ε\lvert{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[F_{1}({\hat{\theta}})-{F^{*}}\right]\rvert\leq{\varepsilon} and 𝔼⁡[[F2​(θ^)]+]≤ε{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}({\hat{\theta}})]_{+}\right]\leq{\varepsilon}, where ε>0{\varepsilon}>0. At first sight, optimizing (CME) over θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, rather than directly over all stationary policies, may appear restrictive. The following proposition shows that the (anchored) tabular softmax family is dense in the set of stationary policies. Theorem 0.C.2 (Appendix) then shows that this density is sufficient for the stated approximate objective and feasibility guarantees.

Proposition 4.1 (Anchored Softmax Approximation of Stationary Policies).

Let 𝕄{\mathbb{M}} be a finite MDP with an initial distribution mins∈𝒮⁡μ0​(s)>0\min_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\mu_{0}({s})>0, and fix a reference action a0∈𝒜{a}_{0}\in{\mathcal{A}}. Consider the anchored tabular logits ψ⁡(s,a0,θ)=0\psi({s},{a}_{0};\theta)=0 and ψ⁡(s,a,θ)=θs,a\psi({s},{a};\theta)=\theta_{{s},{a}} for a≠a0{a}\neq{a}_{0}, with parameter space ΘR=[−R,R]𝒮×(𝒜∖{a0})\Theta_{R}=[-R,R]^{{\mathcal{S}}\times({\mathcal{A}}\setminus\{{a}_{0}\})}. For every stationary policy π∗∈Π\pi^{*}\in\Pi, including deterministic ones, and every ε∈(0,1]{\varepsilon}\in(0,1], there exist R=𝒪⁡(log⁡(|𝒜|/ε))R={\OOSym\!\left(\log(\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|/{\varepsilon})\right)} and a parameter θ∈ΘR\theta\in\Theta_{R} such that

maxs∈𝒮∥πθ(⋅|s)−π∗(⋅|s)∥1≤ε,\displaystyle\max_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\;\lVert\pi_{\theta}(\,\cdot\,{}|{s})-\pi^{*}(\,\cdot\,{}|{s})\rVert_{1}\leq{\varepsilon},

i.e. the family of anchored tabular softmax classes ⋃R>0{πθ:θ∈ΘR}\bigcup_{R>0}\{\pi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{R}\} is dense in the set of stationary policies.

Proof.

Full details in Appendix 0.C, we show that fixing the reference logit makes the parameter-to-occupancy map invertible with a Lipschitz inverse on ΘR\Theta_{R}. ∎

The problem formulation (CME) includes, but is not limited to, the following examples:

  • •

    (Cumulative Cost) A safety constraint can be given by the discounted cumulative cost F2​(θ)≔(1−γ)​𝔼μ0,πθ​[∑t=0∞γt​c​(st,at)]−cmaxF_{2}(\theta)\coloneqq(1-\gamma){\mathbb{E}}_{\mu_{0},\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\,c(s_{t},a_{t})\right]-{c_{\max}}, for a cost vector c∈ℝ𝒮×𝒜c\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}}. In this case (CME) corresponds to finding the policy with the maximum entropy among all the policies solving the environment ℛ⁡(λπθ)≔⟨c,λπθ⟩−cmax{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})\coloneqq\langle c,\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}\rangle-{c_{\max}}.

  • •

    (Apprenticeship Learning) Closeness to an expert’s or prior trajectory can be encoded using the KL divergence ℛ(λπθ)≔𝖣𝖪𝖫(λπθ∥λπref)−ℛmax{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})\coloneqq{\klDiv\left(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}\lVert\lambda^{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)}-{\mathcal{R}_{\max}}, with respect to the state-action-occupancy measure of a reference policy λπref\lambda^{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}.

Naturally, our framework can be extended to multiple constraints, by considering a vector-valued ℛ{\mathcal{R}} and dealing with the Jacobian instead of the gradient.

5 Policy Gradient Penalty Method

Our approach proceeds by transforming (CME) into an unconstrained optimization problem through a quadratic penalty reformulation:

minθ∈Θ⁡P⁡(θ)≔−F1​(θ)+β​ℒ​(F2​(θ)),\displaystyle\min_{\theta\in\Theta}P(\theta)\coloneqq-F_{1}(\theta)+\beta{{\mathcal{L}}(F_{2}(\theta))}, (PEN)

where ℒ≔[⋅]+2{\mathcal{L}}\coloneqq{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}}. In Appendix 0.D, we show that for non-smooth constrained hidden convex problems the use of the exact penalty function ℒ⁡(⋅)≔[⋅]+{{\mathcal{L}}(\,\cdot\,{})}\coloneqq[\,\cdot\,]_{+} is favorable for the theoretical analysis. Additionally, for θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} we define the quadratic-penalty optimality value gap as P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ)≔P⁡(θ)+F∗P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta})\coloneqq P({\theta})+{F^{*}}.

(Stochastic) Policy Gradient.

To derive the gradient of a general smooth, convex F:Λ→ℝF:\Lambda\to{\mathbb{R}} with respect to θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta we can use the policy gradient theorem [109] and the chain rule. With Vπθ​(r)=⟨λ⁡(θ),r⟩V^{\pi_{\theta}}({r})=\langle\lambda(\theta),{r}\rangle we have

⊤r=∇θVπθ(r)=(1−γ)𝔼μ0,πθ[∑t=0∞γtr(st,at)∑k=0t∇θlog(πθ(ak|sk))]\displaystyle\begin{aligned} {}^{\top}{r}=\nabla_{\theta}V^{\pi_{\theta}}({r})=(1-\gamma){\mathbb{E}}_{\mu_{0},\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}{r}({s}_{t},{a}_{t})\sum_{k=0}^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log(\pi_{\theta}({a}_{k}|{s}_{k}))\right]\end{aligned} (PG-Thm)

by denoting with ∇θλ​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}\lambda(\theta) the Jacobian of the (vector-valued) mapping λ⁡(θ)\lambda(\theta), we can apply the chain rule and obtain

i.e. we can compute the policy gradient of the objective and the constraint estimating the state-action occupancy measure and then applying the standard REINFORCE [145] estimator using HH-long trajectory truncations

of the truncated policy-gradient ∇θF​(λH​(θ))\nabla_{\theta}F(\lambda_{H}(\theta)). We present in Appendix 0.B, how this translates to approximation guarantees with respect to the true, infinite horizon gradient.

Pseudo-rewards and single-trajectory-batch penalty gradients. A key algorithmic novelty lies in the construction of pseudo-rewards g⋄(k)g^{(k)}_{\diamond}, ⋄∈{O,C}\diamond\in\{O,C\}, introduced in Line 5. In generic stochastic optimization, both, exact and quadratic penalty formulations require applying the (generalized) chain rule through the constraint function, which canonically necessitates separate stochastic estimators for the function value and its (sub-)gradient. This mismatch induces bias and has led prior work on stochastic penalty methods and ALM to either restrict attention to deterministic constraints [62, 117, 118], incur additional sample complexity via multiple gradient or function evaluations per iteration [26, 78, 127] or rely on momentum and variance-tracking schemes to control the resulting bias [73, 68].

Our method fundamentally departs from this paradigm by explicitly exploiting the RL structure of the problem. Leveraging the Policy Gradient Theorem (PG-Thm), we reinterpret gradients of both the objective and the penalty term as policy gradients with respect to constructed pseudo-rewards. This yields the estimator in ( ∇ θ -Est), which allows us to compute a stochastic gradient of the penalized objective using a single trajectory batch, without auxiliary function-value estimation.

Importantly, the occupancy measure is estimated only once from the full batch, and the resulting common pseudo-reward is reused on every trajectory in that same batch. In particular, the quadratic-penalty gradient contains 2β[ℛ(λ)]+∇ℛ(λ)2\beta[{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)]_{+}\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda), whose two factors both depend on the unknown occupancy measure. Using the same trajectory batch to estimate these factors and form the policy-gradient estimate therefore yields a dependent and biased estimator. We show in Lemmas 0.B.2 and 0.B.5 that our pseudo-reward construction controls both truncation and occupancy-estimation bias, as well as the estimator variance, without requiring a model, an exact value function, nested sampling, or auxiliary function evaluations.

5.1 Theoretical Analysis

The key theoretical insight is the hidden convex structure induced by the occupancy-measure formulation. By mapping a policy π\pi to its corresponding occupancy measure, the penalized problem becomes convex and admits a one-step contraction inequality under biased stochastic gradients. Translating this contraction back to policy space allows us to unroll the recursion over iterations, yielding global last-iterate convergence guarantees. We make the following (standard) assumptions:

Assumption 5.1 (Softmax-Parametrization).

The function ψ:𝒮×𝒜×Θ→ℝ\psi:{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\times\Theta\to{\mathbb{R}} satisfies ψ∈C2​(𝒮,𝒜,Θ,ℝ)\psi\in C^{2}({\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{A}},\Theta;{\mathbb{R}}), and there exist constants ℓψ,Lψ>0{\ell_{\psi}},{L_{\psi}}>0 such that (i) max⁡supθ∈Θs∈𝒮,a∈𝒜⁡∥∇θψ​(s,a,θ)∥≤ℓψ\max_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}},{a}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lVert\nabla_{\theta}\psi({s},{a},\theta)\rVert\leq{\ell_{\psi}} and (ii) max⁡supθ∈Θs∈𝒮,a∈𝒜⁡∥∇θ2​ψ​(s,a,θ)∥≤Lψ\max_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}},{a}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lVert\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\psi({s},{a},\theta)\rVert\leq{L_{\psi}}.

Under these assumptions, we show the regularity of the score function ∇θ​log​πθ​(⋅)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(\,\cdot\,{}) in Appendix 0.B.

Assumption 5.2 (Occupancy-Measure Parametrization).

The parameter-to-occupancy mapping λ:Θ→Λ\lambda:\Theta\to\Lambda, θ↦λπθ\theta\mapsto\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}, satisfies:

  • •

    (Locally Invertible) For every parameter θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta there exists a neighborhood θ∈𝒰θ⊂Θ\theta\in\mathcal{U}_{\theta}\subset\Theta such that λπθ|𝒰θ\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}|_{\mathcal{U}_{\theta}} is a bijection between 𝒰θ\mathcal{U}_{\theta} and 𝒱θ≔λπθ​(𝒰θ){\mathcal{V}}_{\theta}\coloneqq\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}(\mathcal{U}_{\theta}). A (local) inverse is λ𝒱θ−1:𝒱θ→𝒰θ\lambda^{-1}_{{\mathcal{V}}_{\theta}}:{\mathcal{V}}_{\theta}\to\mathcal{U}_{\theta}.

  • •

    (Lipschitz Inverse) The inverse λ𝒱θ−1\lambda^{-1}_{{\mathcal{V}}_{\theta}} is μλ{\mu_{\lambda}}-Lipschitz continuous over Θ.\Theta.

  • •

    (Locally Hidden Convex) There exists an ελ>0{\varepsilon}_{\lambda}>0 such that for all ε∈(0,ελ]{\varepsilon}\in(0,{\varepsilon}_{\lambda}] and all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta the convex combination satisfies (1−ε)​λπθ+ε​λπ⋆∈𝒱θ(1-{\varepsilon})\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}+{\varepsilon}\lambda^{\pi^{\star}}\in{\mathcal{V}}_{\theta}.

The above assumption is common and was verified in a tabular setting, e.g., [144, Prop. H.1]. For the (anchored) tabular softmax parametrization above, we verify Assumption 5.1 and Assumption 5.2 directly in Appendix 0.C. Note that since Λ\Lambda is a polytope (Λ⊂[0,1]𝒮×𝒜\Lambda\subset[0,1]^{{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}}), its domain is bounded, i.e., there exists 𝒟Λ>0{\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}}>0 such that ∥λ⁡(θ)−λ⁡(θ′)∥≤𝒟Λ,\lVert\lambda(\theta)-\lambda(\theta^{\prime})\rVert\leq{\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}}, for any θ,θ′∈Θ\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta. Due to the (local) Lipschitzness of the inverse we can also uniformly bound the domain Θ\Theta by a diameter 𝒟Θ{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}, cf. Thm. 3.2 in Zhang et al. [144]

Assumption 5.3 (L-smoothness).

Assume that for ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and ℛ{\mathcal{R}} there exist ℓλ,Lλ,Lλ,∞>0\ell_{\lambda},L_{\lambda},L_{\lambda,\infty}>0 such that G∈{−ℋ,ℛ}G\in\{-{\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{R}}\} satisfies for all λ,λ′∈Λ\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in\Lambda: (i) ∥∇λG​(λ)∥∞≤ℓλ\lVert\nabla_{\lambda}G(\lambda)\rVert_{\infty}\leq\ell_{\lambda}, (ii) ∥∇λG​(λ)−∇λG​(λ′)∥∞≤Lλ​∥λ−λ′∥2\lVert\nabla_{\lambda}G(\lambda)-\nabla_{\lambda}G(\lambda^{\prime})\rVert_{\infty}\leq L_{\lambda}\lVert\lambda-\lambda^{\prime}\rVert_{2}, and (iii) ∥∇λG​(λ)−∇λG​(λ′)∥∞≤Lλ,∞​∥λ−λ′∥1\lVert\nabla_{\lambda}G(\lambda)-\nabla_{\lambda}G(\lambda^{\prime})\rVert_{\infty}\leq L_{\lambda,\infty}\lVert\lambda-\lambda^{\prime}\rVert_{1}.

We want to emphasize that the aforementioned assumptions are standard in convex (constrained) RL, cf. [50, 146, 11, 135, 12]. Strictly spoken, the entropy objective is only locally smooth [50, 146] and in Section 0.C.2 we consider the smoothed alternative ℋσ(λ)≔−∑s,aλ(s,a)log(λ(s,a)+σ){\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}(\lambda)\coloneqq-\sum_{{s},{a}}\lambda({s},{a})\log\bigl(\lambda({s},{a})+\sigma\bigr), for σ>0\sigma>0, explictily deriving the constants above as well as approximation guarantees and strong-duality translation back to the original entropy.

The following main theorem gives a guarantee on the optimality value gap of the penalty function, without the assumption of strong duality.

Theorem 5.4 (Biased SGD for (PEN)).

Let ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 be the target accuracy. Under Assumptions 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, running Section 5 with a step size η=1/LP,θ\eta=\nicefrac{{1}}{{L_{P,\theta}}}, a batch size of B=𝒪~⁡(1ε2+β2ε2)B={\OOTildeSym\!\left(\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}^{2}}+\frac{\beta^{2}}{{\varepsilon}^{2}}\right)} and a trajectory length of H=𝒪⁡(log⁡(1ε+βε))H={\OOSym\!\left(\log\left(\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}+\frac{\beta}{{\varepsilon}}\right)\right)}, we obtain

𝔼⁡[P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ(N))]≤εafterN≥𝒪⁡((1ε+βε)⋅log⁡(P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ(0))ε))=𝒪~⁡(1ε+βε).\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta}^{(N)})\right]\leq{\varepsilon}\quad\text{after}\quad N\geq{\OOSym\!\left(\left(\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}+\frac{\beta}{{\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\log\left(\frac{P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta}^{(0)})}{{\varepsilon}}\right)\right)}={\OOTildeSym\!\left(\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}+\frac{\beta}{{\varepsilon}}\right)}.

iterations, where P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ(0))P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta}^{(0)}) is the initial value gap and LP,θL_{P,\theta} is defined in Corollary 0.B.4.

Proof.

(Sketch) First, our proof establishes the regularity of the penalty objective PP in Lemma 0.B.3 using Assumption 5.3. Next, we analyze Section 5 by controlling the bias and variance of the SGD step, which yields global convergence. A detailed proof is available in Section 0.B.2.1. ∎

The above theorem implies that for any penalty regularization parameter β\beta, Section 5 solves our penalty formulation (PEN) despite the bias of the stochastic gradients occurring from the estimation of the state occupancy measure in ( λ MC H -Est) and propagating to ( ∇ θ -Est). However, the sample complexity N⋅BN\cdot B crucially depends on the parameter β\beta, coming from the estimate of the smoothness constant LP,θ.L_{P,\theta}. In what follows, we will translate the result to convergence to an (ε,ε)({\varepsilon},{\varepsilon})-optimal solution and give a recommendation on the parameter β\beta trading the feasibility and sample complexity. We use the following standard assumption.

Assumption 5.5 (Strong Duality).

We assume strong duality holds for (CME), i.e. for θ∗{\theta}^{*} there exists a Lagrangian multiplier ν∗≥0{\nu^{*}}\geq 0 such that d∗=d⁡(ν∗)=−F∗{d^{*}}=d({\nu^{*}})=-{F^{*}}, where the (Lagrangian) dual function is defined as the infimum of the Lagrangian with respect to the primal variable θ{\theta}, that is, d⁡(ν)≔infθ∈ΘL⁡(θ,ν)=infθ∈Θ(−F1​(θ)+ν​F2​(θ))d(\nu)\coloneqq\inf_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}L({\theta},\nu)=\inf_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}\bigl(-F_{1}({\theta})+\nu F_{2}({\theta})\bigr), and the corresponding dual problem as d∗≔supν≥0d⁡(ν)=supν≥0infθ∈ΘL⁡(θ,ν){d^{*}}\coloneqq\sup_{\nu\geq 0}d(\nu)=\sup_{\nu\geq 0}\inf_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}L({\theta},\nu).

It is well known that, in general for any ν≥0\nu\geq 0, we have d⁡(ν)≤−F∗d(\nu)\leq-{F^{*}}, i.e. weak duality always holds [96]. Assumption 5.5 is not required for convergence to the penalty objective in Theorem 5.4; it is used only for the subsequent translation to objective and feasibility guarantees through a finite multiplier. Most importantly, it is strictly weaker than Slater’s condition: Slater is a sufficient certificate for strong duality [96], but is not necessary. Consequently, strong duality permits boundary-only feasible sets and equality constraints for which Slater fails [45]. Under linear safety or performance constraints, a feasible point is already sufficient, cf. Bertsekas [15, Prop. 5.3.1].

5.2 Sample Complexity Analysis

Under strong duality, we can now translate the results of Theorem 5.4 into guarantees for the optimality value gap and the constraint violation.

Corollary 5.6.

Let ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 be the target accuracy. Under Assumptions 5.1, 5.2, 5.3 and strong duality, Assumption 5.5, running Section 5 with a step size η=𝒪⁡(ε)\eta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}\right)}, a batch size of B=𝒪⁡(ε−4)B={\OOSym\!\left({{\varepsilon}^{-4}}\right)}, a penalty parameter β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)}, and a trajectory length of H=𝒪⁡(log⁡1ε)H={\OOSym\!\left(\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right)}, we obtain

−ε≤𝔼⁡[F1​(θ(N))−F∗]≤εand𝔼⁡[[F2​(θ(N))]+]≤ε\displaystyle-{\varepsilon}\leq{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[F_{1}({\theta}^{(N)})-{F^{*}}\right]\leq{\varepsilon}\quad\text{and}\quad{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}({\theta}^{(N)})]_{+}\right]\leq{\varepsilon}

after N=𝒪~⁡(ε−2)N={\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-2}\right)} iterations, resulting in a total of 𝒪~⁡(ε−6){\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-6}\right)} trajectory rollouts of length 𝒪⁡(log⁡1ε){\OOSym\!\left(\log\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\right)}.33 3 The expectation is with respect to the randomness of the MDP, the policy, and the initial state distribution.

Proof.

(Sketch) Translating the guarantees of Theorem 5.4 under strong duality requires β⁡(ε)≔(ν∗+1)​ν∗+ν∗2+2ε=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta({\varepsilon})\coloneqq({\nu^{*}}+1)\frac{{\nu^{*}}+\sqrt{{\nu^{*}}^{2}+2}}{{\varepsilon}}={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)}, using Corollary 0.D.22. See Section 0.B.2.2 for the full derivation. ∎

In Appendix 0.C.2 we show that working with the smoothed entropy with σ=ε4​|𝒮|​|𝒜|\sigma=\frac{{\varepsilon}}{4\left|{\mathcal{S}}\right|\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|} requires only the original strong-duality assumption and preserves the 𝒪~⁡(ε−6){\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-6}\right)} rollout rate for fixed dimension. Writing d=|𝒮|​|𝒜|d=\left|{\mathcal{S}}\right|\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|, tracking dimension explicitly yields the conservative dependence 𝒪~⁡((d+1)3​ε−6){\OOTildeSym\!\left((d+1)^{3}{\varepsilon}^{-6}\right)}. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first poly⁡(1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(1/{\varepsilon}) sample complexity guarantee for constrained maximum-entropy exploration under general policy parametrization. Crucially, the guarantee is for the last iterate of a single-loop algorithm and applies simultaneously to the objective and constraint in (CME). The choice β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)} follows from the strong-duality translation, reflecting the scaling between feasibility enforcement and the dual multiplier. A limitation of the current analysis is the large batch size B=𝒪⁡(ε−4)B={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-4}\right)}, required to control truncation bias and occupancy-measure estimation. We expect this can be reduced, for example via variance reduction techniques [146, 11, 43]; indeed, the ablations in the next section suggest the ε−4{\varepsilon}^{-4} dependence is likely conservative in practice. A sharper theoretical analysis is left for future work.

6 Numerical Experiments

We validate our method in a FrozenLake grid-world environments which is visualized in Figure 5(a), where the experiment involves maximizing the entropy while fulfilling a (linear) safety constraint. The full details and additional experiments with a non-linear norm constraint are deferred to Appendix 0.E. All training curves report the mean and one standard deviation across seeds; the grid-world experiments use 10 seeds and the continuous experiments use 5 seeds each.

6.1 Theoretical Setting: Grid World

We compare our approach to the primal-dual (PDPG) algorithm of Ying et al. [135] for which we performed a hyperparameter search (details in Section 0.E.1) and display their best-performing model in Figure 2. While our PGP-method achieves an objective function slightly below the unconstrained maximum entropy policy and meets the safety constraints, the primal-dual version exhibits weak regret in practice: the iterates oscillate around the constraint, cf. [88, Sec. 6]. This distinction persists throughout late training: over the final 1000 epochs, highlighted by the pink region in Figure 2, Table 2 shows that PGP satisfies both feasibility tolerances substantially more often than PDPG.

Figure 2 shows that the proposed penalty formulation is highly robust to the choice of β\beta. Across several orders of magnitude, the achieved entropy remains essentially unchanged once feasibility is reached, while constraint violations decrease monotonically. This indicates that effective constraint enforcement does not require fine-tuning of the penalty parameter and does not trade off against the exploration objective. The checkpoint analysis in Table 1 also quantifies the corresponding cost: once β\beta is sufficiently large for feasibility, further overestimation primarily slows convergence rather than changing the final entropy or constraint value.

6.2 Beyond Theory: Continuous State-Action Space

These experiments assess practical scalability and whether the robustness to gradient noise and the choice of β\beta observed in the finite setting transfers to continuous state-action spaces. Extending our theoretical analysis to this setting is an important direction for future work. The main challenge in the continuous setting lies in estimating approximating the state-action occupancy measure. We address this using the current state-of-the-art maximum-likelihood estimator of Barakat et al. [12], with technical details deferred to Section 0.E.3.

Imitation Learning Constraint.

We train a reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} using the Soft-Actor Critic (SAC) method [101] to solve the PointMass environment [41]. We then apply our method to (CME) with an apprenticeship constraint ℛ(λπθ)≔𝖣𝖪𝖫(λπθ∥λπref)−ℛmax≤0{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})\coloneqq{\klDiv\left(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}\lVert\lambda^{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)}-{\mathcal{R}_{\max}}\leq 0. Figure 3 illustrates the central tension of this setting: the reference policy consistently directs the agent toward the center of the environment, inherently discouraging exploration. As the constraint budget ℛmax{\mathcal{R}_{\max}} increases, the learned policy is permitted greater deviation from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and progressively overcomes this bias, achieving increasingly uniform coverage of the state space. We visualize the controls for different starting positions and varying ℛmax{\mathcal{R}_{\max}} in Figure 14 (Appendix).

Reward Constraint.

The SafeCartpole task [41] imposes a (linear) symmetric box constraint ℛ⁡(λπθ)≔⟨cpos,λπθ⟩−cmax≤0{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})\coloneqq\langle c_{\mathrm{pos}},\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}\rangle-{c_{\max}}\leq 0 on the cart position, making exploration structurally challenging. Effective exploration requires a swing-up, which must be executed within tight positional bounds. Figure 4(a) quantifies this tension: increasing entropy, necessary for swing-up, systematically drives constraint violations toward the safety threshold, with PGP successfully navigating this tradeoff (Figure 4(b)). Compared with the tuned PDPG baseline, PGP maintains sustained swing-up and feasibility substantially more consistently over the final 500 epochs, cf. pink region \scriptsize2⃝ in Figure 4(a) and quantified in Table 2. This comparison is practical evidence beyond the scope of our finite-space theorem. The policy snapshots (vertical lines in Figure 4(a)) trace the training dynamics in Figure 17 (Appendix): early iterations focus on swing-up, intermediate policies exploit symmetry for broader state-space coverage, and later stages approach the constraint boundary to minimize swing-up time while maintaining feasibility. A detailed quantitative analysis is provided in Section 0.E.3.3.

7 Concluding Remarks & Future Work

We propose a single-loop, policy-space penalty method for constrained maximum-entropy exploration. Our analysis provides global last-iterate convergence guarantees under strong duality, despite non-convex policy parameterization and stochastic gradients, and we demonstrate the scalability of our method on a continuous control task. Future work includes extensions to non-smooth occupancy-measure constraints. On the algorithmic side, closing the theory-practice gap in step-size and batch-size selection remains an important and non-trivial challenge. Finally, our current algorithm and analysis yield a relatively large 𝒪~​(ε−6)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}({\varepsilon}^{-6}) sample complexity. We believe this sample complexity can be reduced by using additional algorithmic refinements, such as variance reduction or adaptive penalty schemes. However, a rigorous validation of these directions remains open.

Appendix 0.A Additional Related Work

We provide additional related work and make precise why our contributions are substantively different from the two most closely related works.

Different Entropy Formulations.

Other works deal with Rényi entropy formulation [141, 136], geometric aware Shannon entropy [49], and f-Divergence entropy regularization [3]. Lee et al. [67], Islam et al. [53] recast exploration in terms of marginal state distribution learning, while Jain et al. [55] focus on entropy maximization of a single trajectory, Zamboni et al. [140] on a multi-agent RL setting, and Zisselman et al. [148] use ensemble agents to ensure exploration at test-time.

Optimization Literature.

Our algorithmic framework is most closely related to penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods (ALM) for constrained optimization. Such methods are classical tools with a long history and broad adoption [25, 46, 14, 20, 96], and have been extensively studied from a first-order complexity perspective in both convex and non-convex settings [8, 64, 94, 71]. However, existing analyses typically focus on deterministic optimization, establish asymptotic convergence or convergence to ε{\varepsilon}-KKT points, and do not directly apply to entropy-based reinforcement learning, where non-convexity arises from policy parameterization and gradients are estimated stochastically.

Recent work has also highlighted naively incorporating constraints as costs in the objective function may fail to simultaneously ensure feasibility and optimality in deep learning settings [102]. Our results demonstrate that, when combined with problem-specific gradient structure, quadratic penalty methods can yield strong guarantees even in stochastic, non-convex RL problems. A unified view connecting our approach to proximal-point and ALM frameworks under hidden convexity is developed in Appendix 0.D.

0.A.1 Detailed Comparison to Zhang et al. [144]

Problem.

Zhang et al. [144] study unconstrained general-utility RL, i.e., maximizing a convex functional F⁡(λπ)F(\lambda^{\pi}) without constraints; introducing constraints changes the optimization landscape fundamentally. Moreover, Example 2.1 therein is restricted to cumulative discounted reward in a standard constrained MDP via a generic penalty function, leaving both the concrete choice of penalty and the specific objective unspecified.

Algorithm.

The core algorithmic novelty is not in running biased SGD per se, but in how we construct the gradient estimator for the penalized objective. In generic stochastic penalty and ALM methods, the chain rule through β​[ℛ⁡(λ⁡(θ))]+2\beta\,{[{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda(\theta))]_{+}^{2}} canonically requires separate stochastic estimators for the constraint function value ℛ⁡(λ⁡(θ)){\mathcal{R}}(\lambda(\theta)) and its sub-gradient; their product creates a cross-term bias that does not vanish with batch size. This fundamental bias mismatch has forced the prior stochastic penalty and ALM methods to either (i) restrict to deterministic constraints, (ii) use nested sampling or multiple gradient evaluations per iteration, or (iii) rely on momentum or variance-tracking. Our pseudo-reward construction (Line 5 of Section 5) circumvents this entirely by reinterpreting both gradient terms as policy gradients with respect to constructed pseudo-rewards via the Policy Gradient Theorem. This construction is specific to the RL structure and does not appear in, and cannot be derived from, Zhang et al. [144], which operates in the unconstrained setting.

Theory.

Zhang et al. [144] explicitly assume exact knowledge of the Q-function (cf. the Remark after their Theorem 2); our analysis operates in the realistic stochastic setting, requiring a joint control of truncation bias 𝒪⁡(γH)\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{H}) and Monte-Carlo variance 𝒪(B−1/2)\mathcal{O}(B^{-1/2}) (cf. Lemma 0.B.2). Beyond this stochastic extension, two further nontrivial analytical steps are required:

  • •

    Preservation of hidden convexity under the penalty (Lemma 0.B.3): Showing that composing ℛ⁡(λ)\mathcal{R}(\lambda) with the quadratic penalty [⋅]+2[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2} preserves the smoothness and hidden convexity structure, and deriving the β\beta-dependent smoothness constants (ℓP,λ,LP,λ,LP,λ,∞)(\ell_{P,\lambda},L_{P,\lambda},L_{P,\lambda,\infty}), requires careful analysis of the interaction between the penalty nonlinearity and the occupancy-measure geometry. We are not aware of any prior work establishing such a result.

  • •

    Translation under strong duality (Corollary 5.6, Corollary 0.D.22): Converting the penalty gap P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ(N))≤εP^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta^{(N)}})\leq{\varepsilon} into simultaneous objective and constraint guarantees requires a quantitative relationship between β⁡(ε)\beta(\varepsilon) and the dual multiplier η∗\eta^{*}. This translation, yielding the specific scaling β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1}), is new to hidden convex optimization.

0.A.2 Detailed Comparison to Fatkhullin et al. [44]

Fatkhullin et al. [44] analyze unconstrained stochastic optimization under hidden convexity with an unbiased gradient oracle. Thus constraints, stochastic biased gradients, and their interaction with hidden convexity are not addressed therein. We borrow the hidden-convexity framework but face two difficulties absent in Fatkhullin et al. [44].

  • •

    First, our gradient estimator introduces bias through two distinct mechanisms: (i) trajectory truncation at horizon HH, and (ii) the occupancy-measure estimation error propagated through the penalty gradient via the pseudo-rewards, which are evaluated at the estimated occupancy measure λ^{\widehat{\lambda}} rather than the true λH\lambda_{H}.

  • •

    Second, the penalty introduces a composite structure whose chain rule canonically induces two independently estimated quantities which we resolve by introducing our pseudo-reward construction.

Controlling the chain of penalty smoothness preservation, through occupancy-measure error propagation, to the final bias-variance tradeoff, is the technical core of our analysis beyond a direct adaptation of Fatkhullin et al. [44] and requires carefully balancing the horizon HH, batch size BB, as well as the the step-size η\eta is a three-way trade-off absent from the unbiased oracle model of Fatkhullin et al. [44].

Furthermore, translating the penalty guarantees to the constrained problem requires the scaling β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)} from strong duality (Assumption 5.5), a condition entirely absent in the unconstrained framework. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work handles the combination of hidden convex constraints and stochastic biased gradients.

In this section, we will derive the bias and the variance of our gradient estimator ( ∇ θ -Est) for F∈{ℋ,ℛ}F\in\{{\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{R}}\}.     ‖λπθ1−λπθ2‖1\displaystyle\left\lVert\lambda^{\pi_{\theta_{1}}}-\lambda^{\pi_{\theta_{2}}}\right\rVert_{1} ≤2​ℓψ1−γ​∥θ1−θ2∥\displaystyle\leq\frac{2\ell_{\psi}}{1-\gamma}\lVert\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\rVert

    LF,θ≔4​Lλ,∞​ℓψ2(1−γ)2+4​(1+γ)​ℓλ​ℓψ2(1−γ)2+2​ℓλ​(Lψ+ℓψ2)1−γ.\displaystyle L_{F,\theta}\coloneqq\frac{4L_{\lambda,\infty}\ell_{\psi}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}+\frac{4(1+\gamma)\ell_{\lambda}\ell_{\psi}^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}+\frac{2\ell_{\lambda}(L_{\psi}+\ell_{\psi}^{2})}{1-\gamma}.
Proof.

See Lem. H.1 in Barakat et al. [11] and Lem. 5.3 in Zhang et al. [146]. In particular, using

(1−γ)​∑t=0∞(t+1)​γt=11−γ,(1−γ)​∑t=0∞(t+1)2​γt=1+γ(1−γ)2,\displaystyle(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}(t+1)\gamma^{t}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma},\quad(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}(t+1)^{2}\gamma^{t}=\frac{1+\gamma}{(1-\gamma)^{2}},

gives the stated gradient and occupancy Lipschitz bounds. Applying the chain rule to F∘λF\circ\lambda, the Lipschitz variation of ∇λF\nabla_{\lambda}F gives the first term in LF,θL_{F,\theta}, while the squared-score and score-Hessian terms give the second and third terms, respectively. ∎

The following lemma allows us to run (biased) SGD as a solver for the unconstrained penalty problem.

Lemma 0.B.2 (Gradient Estimator: Bias and Variance).

Under Assumption 5.1 and Assumption 5.3, the full-batch gradient estimator g^H,B​(∇λF,θ,(τi)i∈[B]){\hat{g}}_{H,B}(\nabla_{\lambda}F,\theta,(\tau_{i})_{i\in[B]}) in ( ∇ θ -Est) satisfies, for every θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta,

‖𝔼⁡[g^H,B​(∇λF,θ,(τi)i∈[B])]−∇θF​(λ⁡(θ))‖\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[{\hat{g}}_{H,B}(\nabla_{\lambda}F,\theta,(\tau_{i})_{i\in[B]})\right]-\nabla_{\theta}F(\lambda(\theta))\right\rVert ≤DH​γH+Dg^B,\displaystyle\leq D_{H}\gamma^{H}+\frac{D_{{\hat{g}}}}{\sqrt{B}},
𝔼⁡[‖𝔼⁡[g^H,B​(∇λF,θ,(τi)i∈[B])]−g^H,B​(∇λF,θ,(τi)i∈[B])‖2]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\left\lVert{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[{\hat{g}}_{H,B}(\nabla_{\lambda}F,\theta,(\tau_{i})_{i\in[B]})\right]-{\hat{g}}_{H,B}(\nabla_{\lambda}F,\theta,(\tau_{i})_{i\in[B]})\right\rVert^{2}\right] ≤σH2B,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sigma_{H}^{2}}{B},

where

DH\displaystyle D_{H} ≔2​ℓψ​[Lλ,∞1−γ+ℓλ​(H+1+γ1−γ)],\displaystyle\coloneqq 2\ell_{\psi}\left[\frac{L_{\lambda,\infty}}{1-\gamma}+\ell_{\lambda}\left(H+1+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\right)\right],
κH\displaystyle\kappa_{H} ≔2​ℓψ​(1−γ)​∑t=0H−1(t+1)​γt≤2​ℓψ1−γ,\displaystyle\coloneqq 2\ell_{\psi}(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}(t+1)\gamma^{t}\leq\frac{2\ell_{\psi}}{1-\gamma},

Importantly, the same trajectory batch is used in the occupancy estimate and in the REINFORCE term, i.e. no independence between these two quantities is assumed.

Proof.

For any fixed pseudo-reward r{r} with ∥r∥∞≤ℓλ\lVert{r}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\ell_{\lambda}, the normalized policy-gradient expansion satisfies

‖𝔼⁡[gH​(θ,τ,r)]‖≤2​ℓψ1−γ​∥r∥∞.\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[g_{H}(\theta,\tau,{r})\right]\right\rVert\leq\frac{2\ell_{\psi}}{1-\gamma}\lVert{r}\rVert_{\infty}.

Set qH≔∇λF​(λH​(θ))q_{H}\coloneqq\nabla_{\lambda}F(\lambda_{H}(\theta)) and q≔∇λF​(λ⁡(θ))q\coloneqq\nabla_{\lambda}F(\lambda(\theta)). Adding and subtracting [∇θλH​(θ)]⊤​q[\nabla_{\theta}\lambda_{H}(\theta)]^{\top}q gives

∇θF​(λH​(θ))−∇θF​(λ⁡(θ))=[∇θλH​(θ)]⊤​(qH−q)+([∇θλH​(θ)]⊤−[∇θλ​(θ)]⊤)​q.\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}F(\lambda_{H}(\theta))-\nabla_{\theta}F(\lambda(\theta))=[\nabla_{\theta}\lambda_{H}(\theta)]^{\top}(q_{H}-q)+\left([\nabla_{\theta}\lambda_{H}(\theta)]^{\top}-[\nabla_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)]^{\top}\right)q.

The first term is the pseudo-reward approximation error, while the second is the truncation tail for the fixed pseudo-reward qq. Using ∥λ−λH∥1=γH\lVert\lambda-\lambda_{H}\rVert_{1}=\gamma^{H} for the pseudo-reward error and bounding the omitted fixed-reward tail gives

‖∇θF​(λH​(θ))−∇θF​(λ⁡(θ))‖≤2​ℓψ​Lλ,∞1−γ​γH+2​ℓψ​ℓλ​(1−γ)​∑t=H∞(t+1)​γt=DH​γH.\displaystyle\left\lVert\nabla_{\theta}F(\lambda_{H}(\theta))-\nabla_{\theta}F(\lambda(\theta))\right\rVert\leq\frac{2\ell_{\psi}L_{\lambda,\infty}}{1-\gamma}\gamma^{H}+2\ell_{\psi}\ell_{\lambda}(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=H}^{\infty}(t+1)\gamma^{t}=D_{H}\gamma^{H}.

For each trajectory τi\tau_{i}, define its normalized empirical occupancy and its trajectory-wise linear policy-gradient operator by

Xi≔(1−γ)​∑t=0H−1γt​δst(i),at(i),𝖬i​r≔gH​(θ,τi,r).\displaystyle X_{i}\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\delta_{{s}_{t}^{(i)},{a}_{t}^{(i)}},\quad\mathsf{M}_{i}{r}\coloneqq g_{H}(\theta,\tau_{i},{r}).

X¯B\displaystyle\bar{X}_{B} ≔1B​∑i=1BXi,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}X_{i}, 𝖬¯B\displaystyle\bar{\mathsf{M}}_{B} ≔1B​∑i=1B𝖬i,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathsf{M}_{i}, 𝖬\displaystyle\mathsf{M} ≔𝔼⁡[𝖬i],\displaystyle\coloneqq{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\mathsf{M}_{i}\right],

𝖬​r=[∇θλH​(θ)]⊤​r.\displaystyle\mathsf{M}{r}=[\nabla_{\theta}\lambda_{H}(\theta)]^{\top}{r}.

𝔼⁡[∥X¯B−λH∥22]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\lVert\bar{X}_{B}-\lambda_{H}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right] =1B​𝔼​[∥X1−λH∥22]=1B​(𝔼⁡[∥X1∥22]−∥λH∥22)≤1B​𝔼​[∥X1∥12]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\lVert X_{1}-\lambda_{H}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{B}\left({\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\lVert X_{1}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]-\lVert\lambda_{H}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq\frac{1}{B}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\lVert X_{1}\rVert_{1}^{2}\right]

𝔼⁡[‖g^H,B−𝔼⁡[g^H,B]‖2]≤2​κH2​(ℓλ2+Lλ2)B=σH2B,\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\left\lVert{\hat{g}}_{H,B}-{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[{\hat{g}}_{H,B}\right]\right\rVert^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2\kappa_{H}^{2}(\ell_{\lambda}^{2}+L_{\lambda}^{2})}{B}=\frac{\sigma_{H}^{2}}{B},

which proves the variance claim and concludes the proof. ∎

0.B.2 Convergence of Biased SGD for (PEN)

We start with the following auxilary result, yielding the Lipschitz constant of the penalty function’s gradient.

Lemma 0.B.3 (Smoothness and Bounded Gradients of Penalty function in λ\lambda).

With ℒ=[⋅]+2{\mathcal{L}}={[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}}, under Assumption 5.1 and Assumption 5.3, the function λ↦P⁡(λ)=−ℋ⁡(λ)+β​[ℛ⁡(λ)]+2\lambda\mapsto P(\lambda)=-{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda)+\beta{[{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)]_{+}^{2}} fulfills the inequalities of Assumption 5.3 with

ℓP,λ\displaystyle\ell_{P,\lambda} ≔ℓℋ,λ+2​β​ℛ𝖴𝖡​ℓℛ,λ,\displaystyle\coloneqq\ell_{{\mathcal{H}},\lambda}+2\beta{\mathcal{R}_{\mathsf{UB}}}\ell_{{\mathcal{R}},\lambda},
LP,λ\displaystyle L_{P,\lambda} ≔Lℋ,λ+2​β​(ℛ𝖴𝖡​Lℛ,λ+|𝒮|​|𝒜|​ℓℛ,λ2),\displaystyle\coloneqq L_{{\mathcal{H}},\lambda}+2\beta\left({\mathcal{R}_{\mathsf{UB}}}L_{{\mathcal{R}},\lambda}+\sqrt{\left|{\mathcal{S}}\right|\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|}\,\ell_{{\mathcal{R}},\lambda}^{2}\right),

Writing r⁡(λ)=[ℛ⁡(λ)]+r(\lambda)=[{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)]_{+}, the chain rule gives

∇λP​(λ)=−∇λℋ​(λ)+2​β​r​(λ)​∇λℛ​(λ).\displaystyle\nabla_{\lambda}P(\lambda)=-\nabla_{\lambda}{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda)+2\beta r(\lambda)\nabla_{\lambda}{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda).

The gradient bound follows from 0≤r≤ℛ𝖴𝖡0\leq r\leq{\mathcal{R}_{\mathsf{UB}}}. The penalty-gradient difference is bounded by

2​β​r​(λ)​∥∇ℛ​(λ)−∇ℛ​(λ′)∥∞+2​β​|r⁡(λ)−r⁡(λ′)|​∥∇ℛ​(λ′)∥∞.\displaystyle 2\beta r(\lambda)\lVert\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)-\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\prime})\rVert_{\infty}+2\beta\lvert r(\lambda)-r(\lambda^{\prime})\rvert\lVert\nabla{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\prime})\rVert_{\infty}.

Combining these inequalities with the function-specific smoothness constants proves all three claims. ∎

Appendix 0.C Softmax Policy Density and Smoothed Entropy

This section contains two independent results. First, we provide a self-contained policy-class example satisfying the parametrization assumptions of Theorem 5.4. Second, we analyze the smoothed entropy ℋσ{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} and its sample complexity. The smoothing analysis does not rely on the softmax density result, and vice versa.

0.C.1 Anchored softmax density

We work with the anchored direct-softmax parametrization in a finite tabular MDP and compute its occupancy-map constants explicitly.

Proof.

(of Proposition 4.1) Without loss of generality it suffices to consider ε∈(0,1]{\varepsilon}\in(0,1]. Fix the same reference action a0∈𝒜{a}_{0}\in{\mathcal{A}} for every state and, for an arbitrary stationary policy π∗∈Π\pi^{*}\in\Pi, define the full-support approximation

πε∗​(a|s)≔(1−ε2)​π∗​(a|s)+ε2​|𝒜|.\displaystyle\pi^{*}_{{\varepsilon}}({a}|{s})\coloneqq\left(1-\frac{{\varepsilon}}{2}\right)\pi^{*}({a}|{s})+\frac{{\varepsilon}}{2\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|}.

For every s∈𝒮{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}, this construction satisfies ∥πε∗(⋅|s)−π∗(⋅|s)∥1≤ε\lVert\pi^{*}_{{\varepsilon}}(\,\cdot\,{}|{s})-\pi^{*}(\,\cdot\,{}|{s})\rVert_{1}\leq{\varepsilon} and πε∗​(a|s)≥ε/(2​|𝒜|)\pi^{*}_{{\varepsilon}}({a}|{s})\geq{\varepsilon}/(2\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|) for all a∈𝒜{a}\in{\mathcal{A}}. Set the reference logit to zero and, for a≠a0{a}\neq{a}_{0}, and choose

θs,a≔log⁡πε∗​(a|s)πε∗​(a0|s).\displaystyle\theta_{{s},{a}}\coloneqq\log\frac{\pi^{*}_{{\varepsilon}}({a}|{s})}{\pi^{*}_{{\varepsilon}}({a}_{0}|{s})}.

Substitution into the anchored softmax shows that it represents πε∗\pi^{*}_{{\varepsilon}} exactly. Importantly, this anchoring trick does not remove the reference action: its probability is πθ​(a0|s)=[1+∑a≠a0exp⁡(θs,a)]−1>0\pi_{\theta}({a}_{0}|{s})=[1+\sum_{{a}\neq{a}_{0}}\exp(\theta_{{s},{a}})]^{-1}>0; only its redundant logit coordinate is fixed. We use the rescaling to ensure the mapping between the paramter space and the occupancy measure fulfills Assumption 5.2, cf. Lemma 0.C.1. Moreover, |θs,a|≤log⁡(2​|𝒜|/ε)\lvert\theta_{{s},{a}}\rvert\leq\log(2\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|/{\varepsilon}), so one may take R=log⁡(2​|𝒜|/ε)=𝒪⁡(log⁡(|𝒜|/ε))R=\log(2\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|/{\varepsilon})={\OOSym\!\left(\log(\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|/{\varepsilon})\right)}, concluding the proof. ∎

Lemma 0.C.1 (Softmax Parametrization fulfills Assumption 5.1 and 5.2).

Let mins∈𝒮⁡μ0​(s)>0\min_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\mu_{0}({s})>0, fix a reference action a0∈𝒜{a}_{0}\in{\mathcal{A}}, and let ΘR=[−R,R]𝒮×(𝒜∖{a0})\Theta_{R}=[-R,R]^{{\mathcal{S}}\times({\mathcal{A}}\setminus\{{a}_{0}\})} for R>0R>0. Define

ψ⁡(s,a,θ)≔{θs,a,a≠a0,0,a=a0,andπθ​(a|s)≔exp⁡(ψ⁡(s,a,θ))1+∑a′≠a0exp⁡(θs,a′).\displaystyle\psi({s},{a};\theta)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\theta_{{s},{a}},&{a}\neq{a}_{0},\\ 0,&{a}={a}_{0},\end{cases}\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad\pi_{\theta}({a}|{s})\coloneqq\frac{\exp(\psi({s},{a};\theta))}{1+\sum_{{a}^{\prime}\neq{a}_{0}}\exp(\theta_{{s},{a}^{\prime}})}.

Then the parameter-to-occupancy mapping θ↦λπθ\theta\mapsto\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}} satisfies Assumption 5.1 and Assumption 5.2.

Proof.

The anchored score parametrization is linear in θ\theta, with ∥∇θψ​(s,a,θ)∥≤1\lVert\nabla_{\theta}\psi({s},{a};\theta)\rVert\leq 1 and ∇θ2​ψ​(s,a,θ)=0\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\psi({s},{a};\theta)=0. Hence, Assumption 5.1 holds with ℓψ=1\ell_{\psi}=1 and Lψ=0L_{\psi}=0. Let ΛR≔{λπθ:θ∈ΘR}\Lambda_{R}\coloneqq\{\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}:\theta\in\Theta_{R}\}. Since the discounted state occupancy satisfies

dπθ​(s)≔∑a∈𝒜λπθ​(s,a)≥(1−γ)​μ0​(s)>0,\displaystyle d^{\pi_{\theta}}({s})\coloneqq\sum_{{a}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a})\geq(1-\gamma)\mu_{0}({s})>0,

the occupancy measure uniquely determines the policy and its anchored logits through

πθ(a|s)=λπθ​(s,a)∑a′λπθ​(s,a′),θs,a=logλπθ​(s,a)λπθ​(s,a0)(a≠a0).\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}({a}|{s})=\frac{\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a})}{\sum_{{a}^{\prime}}\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a}^{\prime})},\qquad\theta_{{s},{a}}=\log\frac{\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a})}{\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}({s},{a}_{0})}\quad({a}\neq{a}_{0}).

This proves injectivity. To obtain a uniform Lipschitz inverse, note that every component of every λ∈ΛR\lambda\in\Lambda_{R} is bounded below by

mR≔(1−γ)​mins∈𝒮​μ0​(s)​exp⁡(−R)1+(|𝒜|−1)​exp⁡(R)>0.\displaystyle m_{R}\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\min_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\mu_{0}({s})\frac{\exp(-R)}{1+(\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|-1)\exp(R)}>0.

The logarithm is (1/mR)(1/m_{R})-Lipschitz on [mR,1][m_{R},1]; therefore the displayed inverse is Lipschitz on ΛR\Lambda_{R} with a constant depending only on RR, γ\gamma, μ0\mu_{0}, |𝒮|\left|{\mathcal{S}}\right|, and |𝒜|\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|. Finally, ΛR\Lambda_{R} is exactly the intersection occupancy measure polytope with the linear inequalities

exp⁡(−R)​λ​(s,a0)≤λ⁡(s,a)≤exp⁡(R)​λ​(s,a0),s∈𝒮,a≠a0.\displaystyle\exp(-R)\lambda({s},{a}_{0})\leq\lambda({s},{a})\leq\exp(R)\lambda({s},{a}_{0}),\qquad{s}\in{\mathcal{S}},\ {a}\neq{a}_{0}.

Theorem 0.C.2 (Final Complexity Guarantee under Anchored Direct Softmax Parametrization).

Let λ∗\lambda^{*} be the occupancy measure of an optimal stationary, potentially deterministic policy π∗∈Π\pi^{*}\in\Pi of (CME). Let ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 be the target accuracy. Under Assumption 5.3 for the constraint and strong duality, and using the anchored direct-softmax parametrization on ΘR=[−R,R]𝒮×(𝒜∖{a0})\Theta_{R}=[-R,R]^{{\mathcal{S}}\times({\mathcal{A}}\setminus\{{a}_{0}\})}, run Section 5 with a step size η=𝒪⁡(ε)\eta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}\right)}, a batch size B=𝒪⁡(ε−4)B={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-4}\right)}, a penalty parameter β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)}, and a trajectory length H=𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/ε))H={\OOSym\!\left(\log(1/{\varepsilon})\right)}. Then

−ε≤𝔼⁡[ℋ⁡(λπθ(N))−ℋ⁡(λ∗)]≤ε,𝔼⁡[[ℛ⁡(λπθ(N))]+]≤ε\displaystyle-{\varepsilon}\leq{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda^{\pi_{{\theta}^{(N)}}})-{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda^{*})\right]\leq{\varepsilon},\qquad{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{\pi_{{\theta}^{(N)}}})]_{+}\right]\leq{\varepsilon}

after N=𝒪~⁡(ε−2)N={\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-2}\right)} iterations, resulting in a total of 𝒪~⁡(ε−6){\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-6}\right)} trajectory rollouts of length 𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/ε)){\OOSym\!\left(\log(1/{\varepsilon})\right)}.

Proof.

For any two stationary policies, their normalized discounted occupancy measures satisfy

∥λπ−λπ′∥1≤11−γmaxs∈𝒮∥π(⋅|s)−π′(⋅|s)∥1.\displaystyle{\lVert\lambda^{\pi}-\lambda^{\pi^{\prime}}\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\max_{{s}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\lVert\pi(\,\cdot\,{}|{s})-\pi^{\prime}(\,\cdot\,{}|{s})\rVert_{1}.}

Indeed, the changes in the discounted state occupancy and in the conditional policy are bounded by γ​ρ1−γ\frac{\gamma\rho}{1-\gamma} and ρ\rho, respectively, whenever the maximum policy distance on the right-hand side is at most ρ\rho.

(1) Density argument. Choose an approximation accuracy εapp=𝒪~⁡(ε){\varepsilon}_{\rm app}={\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}\right)} sufficiently small. By Proposition 4.1, there are R=𝒪⁡(log⁡(|𝒜|/εapp))R={\OOSym\!\left(\log(\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|/{\varepsilon}_{\rm app})\right)} and π¯∈{πθ:θ∈ΘR}\bar{\pi}\in\{\pi_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{R}\} whose maximum statewise ℓ1\ell_{1}-distance to π∗\pi^{*} is at most εapp{\varepsilon}_{\rm app}. Hence, writing λ¯=λπ¯\bar{\lambda}=\lambda^{\bar{\pi}} and u=εapp/(1−γ)u={\varepsilon}_{\rm app}/(1-\gamma),

∥λ¯−λ∗∥1≤u.\displaystyle{\lVert\bar{\lambda}-\lambda^{*}\rVert_{1}\leq u.}

By Lemma 0.C.1, this anchored policy class satisfies Assumption 5.1 and Assumption 5.2.

(2) Running PGP. The entropy objective is uniformly continuous on the finite-dimensional occupancy simplex. In particular, for d≔|𝒮|​|𝒜|d\coloneqq\left|{\mathcal{S}}\right|\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right|, we have

|ℋ⁡(λ¯)−ℋ⁡(λ∗)|=𝒪⁡(u​log⁡(d/u)).\displaystyle\lvert{\mathcal{H}}(\bar{\lambda})-{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda^{*})\rvert={\OOSym\!\left(u\log(d/u)\right)}.

Moreover, Lipschitz continuity of the constraint and ℛ⁡(λ∗)≤0{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda^{*})\leq 0 give [ℛ⁡(λ¯)]+≤ℓℛ,λ​u[{\mathcal{R}}(\bar{\lambda})]_{+}\leq\ell_{{\mathcal{R}},\lambda}u. Therefore, for the penalty objective P=−ℋ+β​[ℛ]+2P=-{\mathcal{H}}+\beta{[{\mathcal{R}}]_{+}^{2}} we have

P⁡(λ¯)−P⁡(λ∗)≤𝒪⁡(u​log⁡(d/u))+β​ℓℛ,λ2​u2=𝒪⁡(ε),\displaystyle P(\bar{\lambda})-P(\lambda^{*})\leq{\OOSym\!\left(u\log(d/u)\right)}+\beta\ell_{{\mathcal{R}},\lambda}^{2}u^{2}={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}\right)},

where the last equality follows by taking εapp=𝒪~⁡(ε){\varepsilon}_{\rm app}={\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}\right)} and β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)}. Thus the policy-approximation and optimization errors can be split at the target scale. Since the minimum of PP over ΘR\Theta_{R} is no larger than P⁡(λ¯)P(\bar{\lambda}), the penalty-gap argument of Theorem 5.4, followed by the strong-duality translation in Corollary 5.6, gives the claimed objective and constraint bounds.

(3) Complexity. Every occupancy component is bounded away from zero on the compact class ΘR\Theta_{R}, so the entropy constants required by Assumption 5.3 are finite. Using the constants and the convention of Corollary 5.6, the algorithm requires η=𝒪⁡(ε)\eta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}\right)}, B=𝒪⁡(ε−4)B={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-4}\right)}, β=𝒪⁡(ε−1)\beta={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-1}\right)}, H=𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/ε))H={\OOSym\!\left(\log(1/{\varepsilon})\right)}, and N=𝒪~⁡(ε−2)N={\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-2}\right)}. Multiplying NN and BB yields a total of 𝒪~⁡(ε−6){\OOTildeSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-6}\right)} trajectory rollouts. ∎

0.C.2 Smoothed entropy

Lemma 0.C.3 (Smoothed entropy, penalty constants, and dual translation).

Let d≔|𝒮|​|𝒜|d\coloneqq\left|{\mathcal{S}}\right|\left|{\mathcal{A}}\right| and σ∈(0,1]\sigma\in(0,1].
