Appendix 0.D Unified Penalty Framework for Deterministic Smooth and Non-Smooth Constrained Optimization under Hidden Convexity

This section places the proposed Policy Gradient Penalty (PGP) method into a broader optimization perspective. We show that the constrained maximum-entropy exploration problem studied in the main paper is a special instance of a wider class of constrained optimization problems exhibiting hidden convexity, and that our analysis extends naturally to both smooth and non-smooth settings.

In particular, we connect our approach to penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods (ALM), proximal-point methods, and recent developments in (non-)convex optimization under hidden convexity. While these connections are not required to understand or apply the RL algorithm proposed in the main paper, they clarify the generality of our framework and highlight how problem-specific structure enables guarantees that are unavailable to generic penalty or ALM schemes.

Proximal-point Methods and Penalty Methods.

Proximal-point methods (PPM), originally introduced by Moreau [85] and Martinet [83], were later systematically developed and popularized by Rockafellar [103], Rockafellar [104], Rockafellar and Wets [105], with Boyd and Parikh [19] providing a recent overview. In the context of non-smooth and non-convex optimization, PPM appears either implicitly in convergence analyses or explicitly as an algorithmic design principle for unconstrained problems [31, 30, 29, 32, 33, 44], and more recently in primal-only methods for solving non-smooth, non-convex (deterministic) constrained optimization problems [22, 81, 52, 56, 45]. Related ideas have also been explored in multi-agent and game-theoretic settings, e.g., [57] for constrained Markov games.

Penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods are classical tools for constrained optimization, dating back to early variational approaches [25, 46], and have since been widely adopted and studied [14, 131, 20, 96, 123]. A substantial body of work analyzes first-order penalty and ALM schemes with explicit complexity guarantees in convex optimization [8, 64, 99, 65, 94, 79, 126, 147], as well as more recently in non-convex settings [71, 72].

ALM-PPM Hybrids and Hidden Convexity.

The combination of augmented Lagrangian schemes with proximal-point ideas, originally introduced by Auslender et al. [7], has proven particularly effective. Recent work establishes strong complexity guarantees for smooth non-convex optimization [61, 143, 124, 74], as well as for non-smooth but convex problems [35, 114].

As already mentioned in the main part of this work, (CME) is a special instance of a broader class of (deterministic) optimization problems, called hidden convex problems, of the form

minθ∈Θ⁡F1​(θ)≔H1​(c⁡(θ)),s.t. ​F2​(θ)≔H2​(c⁡(θ))≤0,\displaystyle\min_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}\;F_{1}({\theta})\coloneqq H_{1}(c({\theta})),\quad\text{s.t. }F_{2}({\theta})\coloneqq H_{2}(c({\theta}))\leq 0, (HC)

where we use the function c⁡(⋅)c(\,\cdot\,{}) to indicate a more general transformation, beyond the state-action-occupancy measure we studied in the main part of this work. The following central assumption on c⁡(⋅)c(\,\cdot\,{}) is a stronger version of Assumption 5.2, but the analysis can also be carried out under Assumption 5.2, cf. Fatkhullin et al. [45] after Definition 1.

Definition 0.D.1 (Hidden Convexity).

The above problem (HC) is called hidden convex with modulus μc>0\mu_{c}>0, if its components satisfy the following underlying conditions.

  1. 1.

    The domain Λ=c⁡(Θ){\Lambda}=c({\Theta}) is convex, the functions H1,H2:Λ→ℝH_{1},H_{2}:{\Lambda}\to{\mathbb{R}} are convex, i.e. satisfy for i=1,2i=1,2 and for all u,v∈Λu,v\in{\Lambda} and any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]

    Hi​((1−α)​u+α​v)≤(1−α)​Hi​(u)+α​Hi​(v)−(1−α)​α​μH2​∥u−v∥2.\displaystyle H_{i}((1-\alpha){u}+\alpha{v})\leq(1-\alpha)H_{i}({u})+\alpha H_{i}({v})-\frac{(1-\alpha)\alpha\mu_{H}}{2}\lVert{u}-{v}\rVert^{2}. (HC-1)

    Additionally, we assume (HC) admits a solution u∗∈Λ{u}^{*}\in{\Lambda} with its corresponding objective function value F∗≔H1​(u∗)=F1​(c−1​(u∗)){F^{*}}\coloneqq H_{1}({u}^{*})=F_{1}(c^{-1}({u}^{*})). Throughout this appendix, F∗{F^{*}} denotes the minimum which corresponds to −F∗-{F^{*}} from (CME).

  2. 2.

    The map c:Θ→Λc:{\Theta}\to{\Lambda} is invertible and there exists a μc>0\mu_{c}>0 such that for all θ,θ~∈Θ{\theta},{\tilde{\theta}}\in{\Theta} it holds

    ∥c⁡(θ)−c⁡(θ~)∥≥μc​∥θ−θ~∥.\displaystyle\lVert c({\theta})-c({\tilde{\theta}})\rVert\geq\mu_{c}\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert. (HC-2)

If μH>0\mu_{H}>0, we refer to (HC) as (μc,μH)(\mu_{c},\mu_{H})-strongly convex. Note that in this more generic setting, we have μc=1/μλ\mu_{c}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{\mu_{\lambda}}} of Assumption 5.2. We can map (CME) to (HC) via H1=−ℋH_{1}=-{\mathcal{H}} and H2=ℛH_{2}={\mathcal{R}}.

Note that the condition (HC-2) along with Assumption 0.D.4 imply that the domain Θ{\Theta} has bounded diameter 𝒟Θ≤1μc​𝒟Λ{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}\leq\frac{1}{\mu_{c}}{\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}}. For necessary and sufficient conditions for (HC-2), we refer the reader to Fatkhullin et al. [44].

We start this section with two key inequalities for the analysis of gradient-based methods under hidden convexity, then we analyze biased SGD under hidden convexity and afterwards we generalize our penalty method efforts of the main part to non-smooth problems.

0.D.1 Key Inequalities for Analysis under Hidden Convexity

We state the following proposition which is key for deriving global convergence guarantees under hidden convexity.

Proposition 0.D.2 (Fatkhullin et al. [44] Prop. 3).

Let Fi​(⋅)F_{i}(\,\cdot\,{}), i=1,2i=1,2, be hidden convex with μc>0\mu_{c}>0. For any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] and θ,θ~∈Θ{\theta},{\tilde{\theta}}\in{\Theta}, define θα≔c−1​((1−α)​c​(θ)+α​c​(θ~)){\theta}_{\alpha}\coloneqq c^{-1}((1-\alpha)c({\theta})+\alpha c({\tilde{\theta}})), then, for i=1,2i=1,2, the following functional inequality

Fi​(θα)≤(1−α)​Fi​(θ)+α​Fi​(θ~)−(1−α)​α​μH2​∥c⁡(θ)−c⁡(θ~)∥2,\displaystyle F_{i}({\theta}_{\alpha})\leq(1-\alpha)F_{i}({\theta})+\alpha F_{i}({\tilde{\theta}})-\frac{(1-\alpha)\alpha\mu_{H}}{2}\lVert c({\theta})-c({\tilde{\theta}})\rVert^{2}, (HC-FI)

and norm inequality

∥θα−θ∥≤αμc​∥c⁡(θ)−c⁡(θ~)∥.\displaystyle\lVert{\theta}_{\alpha}-{\theta}\rVert\leq\frac{\alpha}{\mu_{c}}\lVert c({\theta})-c({\tilde{\theta}})\rVert. (HC-NI)

hold.

Proof.

The proof is originally presented in Fatkhullin et al. [44] but we recall it here for educational purposes, since it illustrates the core idea of convergence analyses under hidden convexity.

By (strong) convexity of Hi​(⋅)H_{i}(\,\cdot\,{}) and the convexity of the domain Λ{\Lambda}, we have

Fi​(θα)\displaystyle F_{i}({\theta}_{\alpha}) =Fi​(c−1​((1−α)​c​(θ)+α​c​(θ~)))\displaystyle=F_{i}(c^{-1}((1-\alpha)c({\theta})+\alpha c({\tilde{\theta}})))
=Hi​((1−α)​c​(θ)+α​c​(θ~))\displaystyle=H_{i}((1-\alpha)c({\theta})+\alpha c({\tilde{\theta}}))
≤(1−α)​Hi​(c⁡(θ))+α​Hi​(c⁡(θ~))−(1−α)​α​μH2​∥c⁡(θ)−c⁡(θ~)∥2\displaystyle\leq(1-\alpha)H_{i}(c({\theta}))+\alpha H_{i}(c({\tilde{\theta}}))-\frac{(1-\alpha)\alpha\mu_{H}}{2}\lVert c({\theta})-c({\tilde{\theta}})\rVert^{2}
=(1−α)​Fi​(θ)+α​Fi​(θ~)−(1−α)​α​μH2​∥c⁡(θ)−c⁡(θ~)∥2,\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)F_{i}({\theta})+\alpha F_{i}({\tilde{\theta}})-\frac{(1-\alpha)\alpha\mu_{H}}{2}\lVert c({\theta})-c({\tilde{\theta}})\rVert^{2},

using that (1−α)​c​(θ)+α​c​(θ~)∈Λ(1-\alpha)c({\theta})+\alpha c({\tilde{\theta}})\in{\Lambda} for any θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta}, with i=1,2i=1,2.

Using the property of cc we obtain

∥θα−θ∥=∥c−1​((1−α)​c​(θ)+α​c​(θ~))−c−1​(c⁡(θ))∥≤1μc​∥α⁡(c⁡(θ)−c⁡(θ~))∥,\displaystyle\lVert{\theta}_{\alpha}-{\theta}\rVert=\lVert c^{-1}((1-\alpha)c({\theta})+\alpha c({\tilde{\theta}}))-c^{-1}(c({\theta}))\rVert\leq\frac{1}{\mu_{c}}\lVert\alpha(c({\theta})-c({\tilde{\theta}}))\rVert,

which concludes the proof. ∎

0.D.2 Biased Stochastic Gradient Descent under Hidden Convexity

To solve our penalty problem (OptGap), we use (projected) Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with a biased gradient estimate. We analyze biased SGD in our more general, hidden convex setting.

Consider the following general update of projected stochastic gradient descent:

θ(k+1)≔projΘ⁡(θ(k)−η​g(k)),g(k+1)≔g^(k+1)​(θ(k),ξ(k)),\displaystyle{\theta}^{(k+1)}\coloneqq\proj_{{\Theta}}\left({\theta}^{(k)}-\eta g^{(k)}\right),\quad g^{(k+1)}\coloneqq\hat{g}^{(k+1)}({\theta}^{(k)},\xi^{(k)}), (SGD)

where the stochastic gradient oracle satisfies

𝔼ξ​[g^(k)​(θ,ξ)]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}\!\left[\hat{g}^{(k)}({\theta},\xi)\right] =∇θF​(θ)+b⁡(θ)\displaystyle=\nabla_{{\theta}}F({\theta})+b({\theta}) (SGD-Bias)
𝔼ξ​[‖g^(k)​(θ,ξ)−𝔼ξ​[g^(k)​(θ,ξ)]‖2]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}\!\left[\left\lVert\hat{g}^{(k)}({\theta},\xi)-{\mathbb{E}}_{\xi}\!\left[\hat{g}^{(k)}({\theta},\xi)\right]\right\rVert^{2}\right] ≤σ2\displaystyle\leq\sigma^{2} (SGD-Var)

with variance σ2≥0\sigma^{2}\geq 0 and a uniformly bounded bias ‖b⁡(θ)‖2≤δ2\left\lVert b({\theta})\right\rVert^{2}\leq\delta^{2}, δ≥0\delta\geq 0, for all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta}.

Theorem 0.D.3 (Biased SGD, Hidden Convexity).

Let FF be LL-smooth and hidden convex with F∗≔F⁡(θ∗){F^{*}}\coloneqq F({\theta}^{*}) for an θ∗∈Θ{\theta}^{*}\in{\Theta}, i.e. F2≡0F_{2}\equiv 0. Then running (projected) biased (SGD), with a step size η≤1L\eta\leq\frac{1}{L}, yields for every K∈ℕK\in{\mathbb{N}} and any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] the following inequality

𝔼⁡[F⁡(θ(N+1))−F∗]≤(1−α)N​Δ0+𝒟Λ2μc2​η​α+η2​1α​(σ2+δ2)\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[F({\theta}^{(N+1)})-{F^{*}}\right]\leq(1-\alpha)^{N}\Delta_{0}+\frac{{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}}{{\mu^{2}_{c}}\eta}\alpha+\frac{\eta}{2}\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\sigma^{2}+\delta^{2}\right)

with Δ0≔𝔼⁡[F⁡(θ(0))−F∗]\Delta_{0}\coloneqq{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[F({\theta}^{(0)})-{F^{*}}\right]. In particular, for an arbitrary target accuracy of ε>0{\varepsilon}>0, without loss of generality ε≤3​𝒟Λ2​Lμc2{\varepsilon}\leq\frac{3{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}L}{{\mu^{2}_{c}}}, by picking

α≤μc2​η𝒟Λ2​ε3≤μc2𝒟Λ2​L​ε3\displaystyle\alpha\leq\frac{{\mu^{2}_{c}}\eta}{{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}}\frac{{\varepsilon}}{3}\leq\frac{{\mu^{2}_{c}}}{{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}L}\frac{{\varepsilon}}{3}

after

N≥1α​log⁡(3​Δ0ε)≥3​𝒟Λ2⋅Lμc2​1ε​log⁡(3​Δ0ε)\displaystyle N\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\log\left(\frac{3\Delta_{0}}{{\varepsilon}}\right)\geq\frac{3{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}\cdot L}{{\mu^{2}_{c}}}\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}\log\left(\frac{3\Delta_{0}}{{\varepsilon}}\right)

steps, the last iterate satisfies

𝔼⁡[F⁡(θ(N+1))−F∗]≤2​ε3+η2​1α​(σ2+δ2).\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[F({\theta}^{(N+1)})-{F^{*}}\right]\leq\frac{2{\varepsilon}}{3}+\frac{\eta}{2}\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\sigma^{2}+\delta^{2}\right).

Consequently, we need the bias and the variance to satisfy

σ2,δ2≤ε3​αη≤μc29​𝒟Λ2​ε2\displaystyle\sigma^{2},\delta^{2}\leq\frac{{\varepsilon}}{3}\frac{\alpha}{\eta}\leq\frac{{\mu^{2}_{c}}}{9{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}}{\varepsilon}^{2}

in order to get ε{\varepsilon}-close to the global minima.

Proof.

We use Thm. 7 in Fatkhullin et al. [44] and that the gradient estimation error can be uniformly bounded by

𝔼⁡[‖g^(k)−∇F​(θ)‖2]=𝔼⁡[‖g^(k)−𝔼⁡[g^(k)]‖2]+𝔼⁡[‖𝔼⁡[g^(k)]−∇F​(θ)‖2]≤σ2+δ2.\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\left\lVert\hat{g}^{(k)}-\nabla F({\theta})\right\rVert^{2}\right]={\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\left\lVert\hat{g}^{(k)}-{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\hat{g}^{(k)}\right]\right\rVert^{2}\right]+{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\left\lVert{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\hat{g}^{(k)}\right]-\nabla F({\theta})\right\rVert^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}+\delta^{2}.

Plugging this bound into the proof of Thm. 7 in Fatkhullin et al. [44], unrolling the recursion and choosing α\alpha as proposed concludes the proof. ∎

0.D.3 Inexact Proximal Point Penalty Method (IPPPM)

Inspired by the success of the penalty method for solving (CME), the question arises if penalty methods can be used to solve the broader class of constrained hidden convex optimization problems.

Assumption 0.D.4.

We conduct our analysis under the following (standard) assumptions:

  • •

    (Weak Convexity) F1,F2F_{1},F_{2} to be ρ\rho-weakly convex, for an ρ>0\rho>0. It is known that weak convexity is a relatively mild assumption, compared to e.g. smoothness [29, 40]. FiF_{i} is weakly convex, if e.g. FiF_{i} is twice continuously differentiable with the Hessian satisfying ∇2Fi​(θ)≽−ρ\nabla^{2}F_{i}({\theta})\succcurlyeq-\rho, for all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta}, i=1,2i=1,2, cf. Prop 4.12 in Vial [115].

  • •

    (Bounded [Sub-]Gradients) The functions FiF_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, are continuous and satisfy for all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} that ∂Fi​(θ)≠∅\partial F_{i}({\theta})\neq\emptyset and with ∥g∥≤G\lVert g\rVert\leq G we have a uniform bound for all sub-gradients g∈∂Fi​(θ)g\in\partial F_{i}({\theta}), θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta}.

  • •

    (Bounded Domain) The Domain Λ{\Lambda} has a bounded diameter 𝒟Λ>0{\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}}>0.

In particular in the context of non-convex, non-smooth optimization, the proximal point method (PPM) framework [19] has proven to be very successful in the unconstrained setting [31, 28, 29, 30, 32, 44] as well as in the constrained setting [81, 17, 52, 18, 56, 45], either implicitly in the analysis or explicitly for algorithm design. Motivated by the non-smooth literature, as well as recent advances in proximal point method penalty [74] and augmented Lagrangian methods [114, 124], we propose the following, inexact proximal point penalty method:

θ(k)≈θ^(k)≔arg​minθ∈Θ⁡φ(k)​(θ)≔F1​(θ)+ρ^2​∥θ−θ(k)∥2+β​ℒ​(F2​(θ)),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &{\theta}^{(k)}\approx\hat{{\theta}}^{(k)}\coloneqq\argmin_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}{{\varphi}^{(k)}}({\theta})\coloneqq F_{1}({\theta})+\frac{{\hat{\rho}}}{2}\lVert{\theta}-{\theta}^{(k)}\rVert^{2}+\beta{{\mathcal{L}}(F_{2}({\theta}))},\end{aligned} (IPPPM)

where the penalty function ℒ{\mathcal{L}} depends on the smoothness of the constraint. In the case of non-smooth F1,F2F_{1},F_{2}, the exact penalty function [⋅]+[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+} is a natural choice. Under the additional assumption of LL-smooth F1,F2F_{1},F_{2} one needs to “smoothen” the penalty, in order to propagate the smoothness and thus a quadratic penalty [⋅]+2{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}} is applied. For the convergence analysis of IPPM, we use the notation ℒ⁡(⋅){{\mathcal{L}}(\,\cdot\,{})} for both penalty functions and perform a unified analysis by using that both penalty functions are convex and monotone, before we compute the corresponding sample complexities for [⋅]+[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+} and [⋅]+2{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}} individually.

Under Assumption 0.D.4, if ρ^>ρ{\hat{\rho}}>\rho, the inner penalty problem is strongly convex, see Prop. 2.1 in Davis and Grimmer [30].

The roadmap of the PPPM analysis is the following:

  • •

    Preservation of Weak Convexity and Bounded (Sub-)Gradients. Under Assumption 0.D.4, we show in Section 0.D.5 that the penalty term ℒ∘F2{\mathcal{L}}\circ F_{2} has uniformly bounded (sub-)gradients and is weakly convex. Thus, (IPPPM) is ρφ\rho_{\varphi}-weakly convex and can be lifted to be strongly convex. The constant ρφ\rho_{\varphi} depends on the penalty function and the smoothness assumption.

  • •

    Solve inner problem efficiently. We apply an efficient algorithm for the inner (non-)smooth strongly convex unconstrained optimization problems to obtain convergence guarantees for the optimality gap of the penalty function Pℒ,β𝗈𝗉𝗍P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{{\mathcal{L}},\beta}.

  • •

    Translate guarantees. Under the assumption of strong duality, we translate the results into guarantees on the optimality gap and constraint violation. An overview of all of the resulting rates can be found in Table 3.

Assumption 0.D.5 (Unconstrained Solution Oracle).

We assume to have access to an inner approximate solution oracle 𝒜εin{\mathcal{A}}_{{{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{in}}}} to solve (IPPPM) to an εin{{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{in}}}-accuracy in expectation for any εin>0{{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{in}}}>0, i.e.

φpen(k)​(θ(k))−φpen(k)​(θ^(k))≤εin\displaystyle{{\varphi}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{pen}}}({\theta}^{(k)})-{{\varphi}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{pen}}}(\hat{{\theta}}^{(k)})\leq{{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{in}}}

for all iterations k∈[N]k\in[N] after Tin=Tin​(εin){T_{\mathrm{in}}}={T_{\mathrm{in}}}({{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{in}}}) steps.

Exemplarily, for the non-smooth case, we will formulate Corollary 0.D.11 and Corollary 0.D.13 in terms of the classical (stochastic) sub-gradient descent and in the smooth case Corollary 0.D.12 using SGD, respectively.

Remark 0.D.7 (Role of the Penalty Parameter).

It is important to emphasize that, although the parameter β\beta appears only logarithmically in the number of outer iterations NN, it plays a crucial role in shaping the properties of the penalty function. In particular, β\beta affects the norm of the (sub-)gradients, the associated smoothness constant, and consequently the weak convexity parameter. As a result, it directly influences the computational complexity of the inner solver employed for the subproblem.

0.D.3.2 Sample Complexity Analysis

N≥3​β​(ν∗)​ρ​𝒟Λ2μc2​β⁡(ν∗)ε⋅log⁡(3​β​(ν∗)​[Δ0+β⁡(ν∗)​𝒱0]ε)\displaystyle N\geq\frac{3\beta({\nu^{*}})\rho{\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}}{\mu_{c}^{2}}\frac{\beta({\nu^{*}})}{{\varepsilon}}\cdot\log\left(\frac{3\beta({\nu^{*}})[\Delta_{0}+\beta({\nu^{*}}){\mathcal{V}_{0}}]}{{\varepsilon}}\right)

outer iterations yields the guarantee

|F1​(θ(N))−F∗|≤εand[F2​(θ(N))]+≤ε\displaystyle\left\lvert F_{1}({\theta}^{(N)})-{F^{*}}\right\rvert\leq{\varepsilon}\quad\text{and}\quad[F_{2}({\theta}^{(N)})]_{+}\leq{\varepsilon}

as a special case of (IPPPM-Qu). SM has a complexity of

TinSM​(εin)≥12​Gφ2​β​(ν∗)​𝒟Λ2μc2​ε−2=𝒪⁡(ε−2)\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{SM}}({{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{in}}})\geq\frac{12G_{\varphi}^{2}\beta({\nu^{*}}){\mathcal{D}^{2}_{\Lambda}}}{\mu_{c}^{2}}{\varepsilon}^{-2}={\OOSym\!\left({\varepsilon}^{-2}\right)}

to achieve the desired inner accuracy, where Δ0≔F1​(θ(0))−F∗\Delta_{0}\coloneqq F_{1}({\theta}^{(0)})-{F^{*}}, 𝒱0≔[F2​(θ(0))]+{\mathcal{V}_{0}}\coloneqq[F_{2}({\theta}^{(0)})]_{+}, β⁡(ν∗)≔2​ν∗+2\beta({\nu^{*}})\coloneqq 2{\nu^{*}}+2, ρφ​(β)≔β⁡(ν∗)⋅ρ\rho_{\varphi}(\beta)\coloneqq\beta({\nu^{*}})\cdot\rho, and Gφ​(β)≔G+β⁡(ν∗)​ρ​𝒟Θ+β⁡(ν∗)​GG_{\varphi}(\beta)\coloneqq G+\beta({\nu^{*}})\rho{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}+\beta({\nu^{*}})G.

A direct comparison between Corollary 0.D.13 and Corollary 0.D.11 reveals that, in the non-smooth case, the exact penalty function is the natural choice, leading to improved numerical constants since [⋅]+[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+} preserves the weak convexity and the upper bound on the sub-gradients without introducing additional constants.

In contrast, in the smooth case, the quadratic penalty function [⋅]+2{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}} has to be used to smooth the penalty term. While this approach ensures differentiability, it slightly worsens the convergence guarantee compared the results in Fatkhullin et al. [45].

0.D.4 PPPM under Hidden Strong Convexity

In the case of hidden strong convexity, we can significantly strengthen the result of Theorem 0.D.6 to a logarithmic sample complexity in ε−1{\varepsilon}^{-1} for the number of outer loops.

Theorem 0.D.14 (Hidden Strongly Convex, PPPM, Penalty Function).

Assume (HC) is hidden strongly convex with modulus μH>0\mu_{H}>0 and we have access to an oracle 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} according to Assumption 0.D.5. For a target precision ε>0{\varepsilon}>0, lifting parameter ρ^>ρ{\hat{\rho}}>\rho, and a penalty parameter β≥1\beta\geq 1. With the choice of α≔μc2​μHρ^+μc2​μH∈[0,1]\alpha\coloneqq\frac{\mu_{c}^{2}\mu_{H}}{{\hat{\rho}}+\mu_{c}^{2}\mu_{H}}\in[0,1] and for N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, the last iterate of Algorithm 2 satisfies

after

iterations, where Δ0≔F1​(θ^(k))−F∗\Delta_{0}\coloneqq F_{1}(\hat{{\theta}}^{(k)})-{F^{*}} and 𝒱0≔ℒ⁡(F2​(θ(0))){\mathcal{V}_{0}}\coloneqq{{\mathcal{L}}(F_{2}({\theta}^{(0)}))}. 0.D.5 Technical Lemmas

For our penalty approach, we are generally interested in weak convexity of the penalty term, a (generalized) chain rule as well as bounded sub-gradients and LL-smoothness respectively. For the chain rule in the smooth case, we use the result of Drusvyatskiy and Paquette [40], and in the non-smooth case we generalize their results to both, the special case of the quadratic penalty [⋅]+2{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}} and the exact penalty [⋅]+[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}.

Before we start analyzing the two cases separately, we state a few utility Lemmas.

Lemma 0.D.15 (Lipschitz Continuity, Quadratic Penalty).

Let h:𝒴→ℝ,θ~↦[θ~]+2h:{\mathcal{Y}}\to{\mathbb{R}},{\tilde{\theta}}\mapsto{[{\tilde{\theta}}]_{+}^{2}}, 𝒴⊂ℝm{\mathcal{Y}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{m}, m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}} be the quadratic penalty function over a 𝒟𝒴{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{Y}}}-bounded domain. Then hh is 2⋅𝒟𝒴2\cdot{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{Y}}}-Lipschitz continuous.

Furthermore, if composed with a GfG_{f}-Lipschitz continuous function f:Θ→ℝmf:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{m}, over a 𝒟Θ{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}-bounded, compact domain Θ⊂ℝd{\Theta}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, the resulting function h∘fh\circ f is 2⋅𝒟Θ⋅Gf22\cdot{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}\cdot G_{f}^{2}-Lipschitz continuous.

Proof.

We first consider only the quadratic norm. Since we assume to have a feasible point for our problem (HC), we can assume that 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} contains the origin. More generally, one would obtain 2​supv∈𝒴∥[v]+∥2\sup_{{v}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\lVert[{v}]_{+}\rVert as a Lipschitz constant.

The penalty function is globally 2⋅𝒟𝒴2\cdot{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{Y}}}-Lipschitz continuous. I.e. for v,w∈Im⁡(f){v},{w}\in\Image(f) we have

|h⁡(v)−h⁡(w)|=|∥v∥2−∥w∥2|=|⟨v+w,v−w⟩|≤(∥v∥+∥w∥)⋅∥v−w∥,\displaystyle\left\lvert h({v})-h({w})\right\rvert=\left\lvert\lVert{v}\rVert^{2}-\lVert{w}\rVert^{2}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\langle{v}+{w},{v}-{w}\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left(\lVert{v}\rVert+\lVert{w}\rVert\right)\cdot\lVert{v}-{w}\rVert, (12)

which implies 2⋅𝒟Θ2\cdot{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}-Lipschitz continuity on a bounded domain. The same also holds true if we substitute ∥⋅∥2\lVert\,\cdot\,{}\rVert^{2} by [⋅]+2{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}}.

Since ff is Lipschitz continuous and Θ{\Theta} is compact and bounded, also the image 𝒴≔Im⁡(f)≔f⁡(Θ){\mathcal{Y}}\coloneqq\Image(f)\coloneqq f({\Theta}) is compact and bounded by Gf⋅𝒟ΘG_{f}\cdot{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}. Invoking (12) with v=f⁡(θ),w=f⁡(θ~){v}=f({\theta}),{w}=f({\tilde{\theta}}), θ,θ~∈Θ{\theta},{\tilde{\theta}}\in{\Theta}, yields that h∘fh\circ f is (2⋅Gf⋅𝒟Θ⋅Gf)(2\cdot G_{f}\cdot{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}\cdot G_{f})-Lipschitz continuous, concluding the claim. ∎

Lemma 0.D.16 (Weak Convexity of Composition).

Let f:Θ→ℝf:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}}, with Θ⊂ℝd{\Theta}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} bounded and convex, be ρ\rho-weakly convex with a bounded range, and let h:ℝ→ℝh:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} be non-decreasing, convex and GhG_{h}-Lipschitz continuous on range⁡(f)\range(f). Then the composition g≔h∘f:Θ→ℝg\coloneqq h\circ f:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}} is (Gh⋅ρ)(G_{h}\cdot\rho)-weakly convex.

Proof.

To show μ\mu-weak convexity, we need to prove that for all θ,θ~∈Θ{\theta},{\tilde{\theta}}\in{\Theta} and all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] the inequality

g⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~)≤t​g​(θ)+(1−t)​g​(θ~)+μ2​t​(1−t)​∥θ−θ~∥2\displaystyle g(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}})\leq tg({\theta})+(1-t)g({\tilde{\theta}})+\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}

holds. Since by assumption ff is ρ\rho-WC, we know that the function f~​(θ)≔f⁡(θ)+ρ2​∥θ∥2{\tilde{f}}({\theta})\coloneqq f({\theta})+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert{\theta}\rVert^{2} is convex. Let θ,θ~∈Θ{\theta},{\tilde{\theta}}\in{\Theta} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] be arbitrary but fixed. By convexity of f~{\tilde{f}}, we obtain

f⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~)+ρ2​∥t​θ+(1−t)​θ~∥2≤t⁡(f⁡(θ)+ρ2​∥θ∥2)+(1−t)​(f⁡(θ~)+ρ2​∥θ~∥2).\displaystyle f(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}\leq t\left(f({\theta})+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert{\theta}\rVert^{2}\right)+(1-t)\left(f({\tilde{\theta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}\right).

Since the Euclidean norm is 22-strongly convex, we have

∥t​θ+(1−t)​θ~∥2=t​∥θ∥2+(1−t)​∥θ~∥2−t⁡(1−t)​∥θ−θ~∥2.\displaystyle\lVert t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}=t\lVert{\theta}\rVert^{2}+(1-t)\lVert{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}-t(1-t)\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}.

and thus the left-hand side expands to

f⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~)+ρ2​∥t​θ+(1−t)​θ~∥2\displaystyle f(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}
=f⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~)+ρ2​[t​∥θ∥2+(1−t)​∥θ~∥2−t⁡(1−t)​∥θ−θ~∥2].\displaystyle\quad=f(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left[t\lVert{\theta}\rVert^{2}+(1-t)\lVert{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}-t(1-t)\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}\right].

Rearranging yields

f⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~)≤t​f​(θ)+(1−t)​f​(θ~)+ρ2​(1−t)​t​∥θ−θ~∥2⏟≕δ≥0.\displaystyle f(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}})\leq tf({\theta})+(1-t)f({\tilde{\theta}})+\underbrace{\frac{\rho}{2}(1-t)t\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}}_{\eqqcolon\delta\geq 0}.

By inserting the above into hh we obtain

g⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~)\displaystyle g\left(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}}\right) =h⁡(f⁡(t​θ+(1−t)​θ~))\displaystyle=h\left(f(t{\theta}+(1-t){\tilde{\theta}})\right)
≤h⁡(t​f​(θ)+(1−t)​f​(θ~)+δ)\displaystyle{\leq}h\left(tf({\theta})+(1-t)f({\tilde{\theta}})+\delta\right)
≤h⁡(t​f​(θ)+(1−t)​f​(θ~))+Gh⋅δ\displaystyle{\leq}h\left(tf({\theta})+(1-t)f({\tilde{\theta}})\right)+G_{h}\cdot\delta
≤t​h​(f⁡(θ))+(1−t)​h​(f⁡(θ~))+Gh⋅δ\displaystyle{\leq}th\left(f({\theta})\right)+(1-t)h\left(f({\tilde{\theta}})\right)+G_{h}\cdot\delta
=t​g​(θ)+(1−t)​g​(θ~)+Gh⋅ρ2​(1−t)​t​∥θ−θ~∥2\displaystyle{=}tg({\theta})+(1-t)g({\tilde{\theta}})+\frac{G_{h}\cdot\rho}{2}(1-t)t\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert^{2}

by applying in (i)(i) that hh is non-decreasing, in (i​i)(ii) the Lipschitz continuity of hh, and in (i​i​i)(iii) the convexity of hh. This concludes the claim. ∎

0.D.5.1 Smooth Case: Quadratic Penalty

We show that the penalty term is weakly convex, satisfies the chain rule and we give a uniform upper bound for the gradients.

Lemma 0.D.17 (Smooth, Quadratic Penalty).

Let Θ⊂ℝd{\Theta}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} be a 𝒟Θ{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}-bounded, compact domain, and h:ℝ→ℝ,θ↦[θ]+2h:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}},{\theta}\mapsto{[{\theta}]_{+}^{2}} be the quadratic penalty function. We assume that f:Θ→ℝf:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}} is LL-smooth, ρ\rho-weakly convex and has GfG_{f} uniformly bounded gradients. Then the composition g≔h∘f:Θ→ℝg\coloneqq h\circ f:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}} satisfies:

  • •

    (Weak Convexity) The penalty term gg is (2​Gf​𝒟Θ⋅min⁡{ρ,L})(2G_{f}{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}\cdot\min\{\rho,L\})-weakly convex.

  • •

    (Chain Rule) For all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} we have

    ∇g​(θ)=h′​(f⁡(θ))⋅∇f​(θ)=2​[f⁡(θ)]+⋅∇f​(θ).\displaystyle\nabla g({\theta})=h^{\prime}(f({\theta}))\cdot\nabla f({\theta})=2[f({\theta})]_{+}\cdot\nabla f({\theta}).
  • •

    (Bounded Gradients) The gradients of gg are uniformly bounded by Gg≔2​𝒟Θ​Gf2G_{g}\coloneqq 2{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}G_{f}^{2}.

  • •

    (LgL_{g}-smoothness) The penalty term gg is LgL_{g}-smooth, with Lg≔2​(F𝖴𝖡​L+Gf2)L_{g}\coloneqq 2({F_{\mathsf{UB}}}L+G_{f}^{2}),

where maxθ∈Θ⁡|f⁡(θ)|≕F𝖴𝖡<∞\max_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}\lvert f({\theta})\rvert\eqqcolon{F_{\mathsf{UB}}}<\infty is an upper bound.

Proof.

The weak convexity is a consequence of Lemma 0.D.16 and Lemma 4.2 in Drusvyatskiy and Paquette [40]. We apply Lemma 0.D.15 to obtain that gg is Lipschitz continuous. The third claim follows by Theorem 3.1 in Drusvyatskiy and Paquette [40]. To show the LgL_{g}-smoothness, let θ,θ~∈Θ{\theta},{\tilde{\theta}}\in{\Theta}. We have

‖∇g​(θ)−∇g​(θ~)‖\displaystyle\left\lVert\nabla g({\theta})-\nabla g({\tilde{\theta}})\right\rVert ≤2⋅‖[f(θ)]+∇f(θ)−[f(θ)]+∇f(θ~)+[f(θ)]+∇f(θ~)−[f(θ~)]+∇f(θ~)‖\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot\left\lVert[f({\theta})]_{+}\nabla f({\theta})-[f({\theta})]_{+}\nabla f({\tilde{\theta}})+[f({\theta})]_{+}\nabla f({\tilde{\theta}})-[f({\tilde{\theta}})]_{+}\nabla f({\tilde{\theta}})\right\rVert
≤2⋅∥[f(θ)]+(∇f(θ)−∇f(θ~))∥+2⋅∥([f(θ)]+−[f(θ~)]+)∇f(θ~)∥\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot\lVert[f({\theta})]_{+}(\nabla f({\theta})-\nabla f({\tilde{\theta}}))\rVert+2\cdot\lVert([f({\theta})]_{+}-[f({\tilde{\theta}})]_{+})\nabla f({\tilde{\theta}})\rVert
≤2⋅F𝖴𝖡​L​∥θ−θ~∥+2⋅Gf​Gf​∥θ−θ~∥\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot{F_{\mathsf{UB}}}L\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert+2\cdot G_{f}G_{f}\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert
=2​(F𝖴𝖡​L+Gf2)⋅∥θ−θ~∥,\displaystyle=2({F_{\mathsf{UB}}}L+G_{f}^{2})\cdot\lVert{\theta}-{\tilde{\theta}}\rVert,

since for all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} we have [f⁡(θ)]+≤|f⁡(θ)|≤maxθ∈Θ⁡|f⁡(θ)|≕F𝖴𝖡<∞[f({\theta})]_{+}\leq\lvert f({\theta})\rvert\leq\max_{{\theta}\in{\Theta}}\lvert f({\theta})\rvert\eqqcolon{F_{\mathsf{UB}}}<\infty. This concludes the claim. ∎

0.D.5.2 Non-smooth Case: Exact and Quadratic Penalty

We can generalize the result above to the case of non-smooth ff and hh being either the quadratic [⋅]+2{[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}^{2}} or exact penalty [⋅]+[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+}.

Lemma 0.D.18 (Non-Smooth, Quadratic Penalty).

Let f:Θ→ℝf:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}} be a ρ\rho-weakly convex, (potentially) non-smooth, GfG_{f}-Lipschitz continuous function over a 𝒟Θ{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}-bounded domain Θ⊂ℝd{\Theta}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. Furthermore, let h:ℝ→ℝ,θ↦[θ]+2h:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}},{\theta}\mapsto{[{\theta}]_{+}^{2}} be the quadratic penalty function. Then the composition g≔h∘fg\coloneqq h\circ f satisfies:

  • •

    (Weak Convexity) The penalty term gg is (2​Gf​𝒟Θ⋅ρ)(2G_{f}{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}\cdot\rho)-weakly convex.

  • •

    (Generalized Chain Rule) For all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} we have

    ∂g⁡(θ)=2​[f⁡(θ)]+⋅∂f⁡(θ).\displaystyle\partial g({\theta})=2[f({\theta})]_{+}\cdot\partial f({\theta}). (13)
  • •

    (Bounded Sub-gradients) The sub-gradients of gg are uniformly bounded by Gg≔2​𝒟Θ​Gf2G_{g}\coloneqq 2{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}G_{f}^{2}.

Proof.

By Lemma 0.D.15 we know that hh is (2​Gf​𝒟Θ)(2G_{f}{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}})—Lipschitz continuous and the third claim is proved. Consequently, the first claim follows by applying Lemma 0.D.16.

Since gg is weakly convex, it is regular by Proposition 4.4 in Vial [115], according to Definition 3 in Li et al. [69] of regularity, which is by Corollary 8.11 in Rockafellar and Wets [105] equivalent to Definition 6.24 and Corollary 6.29 in Rockafellar and Wets [105] of regularity. Applying the generalized chain rule for sub-gradients, Theorem 10.49 of Rockafellar and Wets [105] and using the fact that hh is continuously differentiable concludes the claim. ∎

Lemma 0.D.19 (Non-Smooth, Exact Penalty).

Let f:Θ→ℝf:{\Theta}\to{\mathbb{R}} be a ρ\rho-weakly convex, (potentially) non-smooth, GfG_{f}-Lipschitz continuous function over a 𝒟Θ{\mathcal{D}_{\Theta}}-bounded domain Θ⊂ℝd{\Theta}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. Furthermore, let h:ℝ→ℝ,θ↦[θ]+h:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}},{\theta}\mapsto[{\theta}]_{+} be the exact penalty function. Then the composition g≔h∘fg\coloneqq h\circ f satisfies:

  • •

    (Weak Convexity) The penalty term gg is ρ\rho-weakly convex.

  • •

    (Generalized Chain Rule) For all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} we have

    ∂g⁡(θ)={∂f⁡(θ),f⁡(θ)>0,[0,1]⋅∂f⁡(θ),f⁡(θ)=0,{0},f⁡(θ)<0,\displaystyle\partial g({\theta})=\begin{cases}\partial f({\theta}),&f({\theta})>0,\\ [0,1]\cdot\partial f({\theta}),&f({\theta})=0,\\ \{0\},&f({\theta})<0,\end{cases} (14)

    with a Minkowski product in the second case.

  • •

    (Bounded Sub-gradients) The sub-gradients of gg are uniformly bounded by Gg≔GfG_{g}\coloneqq G_{f}.

Proof.

If ff is GfG_{f}-Lipschitz, then trivially also h∘fh\circ f is GfG_{f}-Lipschitz. Additionally, [⋅]+[\,\cdot\,{}]_{+} is non-decreasing, convex, and 11-Lipschitz. Thus, the first claim follows by applying Lemma 0.D.16. With the same argument as above, we can apply the generalized chain rule for sub-gradients, Thm. 10.49 in Rockafellar and Wets [105], and obtain

∂θg⁡(θ)=⋃y∈∂h⁡(f⁡(θ))∂(y​f)​(θ),\displaystyle\partial_{\theta}g({\theta})=\bigcup_{y\in\partial h(f({\theta}))}\partial(yf)({\theta}),

with θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta}. To obtain (14), we use the known sub-differential of [θ]+[{\theta}]_{+}:

∂θ[θ]+={{1},θ>0,[0,1],θ=0,{0},θ<0.\displaystyle\partial_{\theta}[{\theta}]_{+}=\begin{cases}\{1\},&{\theta}>0,\\ [0,1],&{\theta}=0,\\ \{0\},&{\theta}<0.\end{cases}

Thus, at f⁡(θ)=0f({\theta})=0, we obtain a convex combination of sub-gradients g∈∂f⁡(θ)g\in\partial f({\theta}) and weights α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]. The result follows. ∎

0.D.6 Strong Duality: Translation of Convergence Guarantees

The challenge in Section 5.1 is the translation of the guarantee on 𝔼⁡[Pℒ,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(⋅)]{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{{\mathcal{L}},\beta}(\,\cdot\,{})\right] to a guarantee on the constraint violation, namely 𝔼⁡[[F2​(⋅)]+]{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}(\,\cdot\,{})]_{+}\right]. The following results show how to perform this translation under strong duality for both, the exact and the quadratic penalty function. For simplicity, we formulate the following corollaries in the deterministic case. Taking expectation yields the desired results.

Lemma 0.D.20 (Upper Bound Constraint Violation).

Let θ∗{\theta}^{*} be the optimal solution of (CME) and assume that strong duality holds, i.e. there exists ν∗≥0{\nu^{*}}\geq 0 such that F∗=d⁡(ν∗){F^{*}}=d({\nu^{*}}). Then we have for all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} the inequality

−ν∗​[F2​(θ)]+≤F1​(θ)−F∗.\displaystyle-{\nu^{*}}[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}\leq F_{1}({\theta})-{F^{*}}.

In particular, for all θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} and any β≥2⋅ν∗\beta\geq 2\cdot{\nu^{*}}, we have

0\displaystyle 0 ≤F1​(θ)−F∗+β​[F2​(θ)]+=P1,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ).\displaystyle\leq F_{1}({\theta})-{F^{*}}+\beta[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}=P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{1,\beta}({\theta}).
Proof.

Lemma 3.1.21 in Nesterov [95]. ∎

Corollary 0.D.21 (Constraint Violation, Exact Penalty).

Assume that for (CME) strong duality holds with a Lagrangian multiplier ν∗≥0{\nu^{*}}\geq 0, and let θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} be a point such that 𝔼⁡[P1,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ)]≤ε{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{1,\beta}({\theta})\right]\leq{\varepsilon} with the exact penalty and β>ν∗\beta>{\nu^{*}}. Then we have the following translation for the constraint violation:

0\displaystyle 0 ≤𝔼⁡[[F2​(θ)]+]≤𝔼⁡[P1,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ)]β−ν∗≤εβ−ν∗.\displaystyle\leq{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}\right]\leq\frac{{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{1,\beta}({\theta})\right]}{\beta-{\nu^{*}}}\leq\frac{{\varepsilon}}{\beta-{\nu^{*}}}.
Proof.

We invoke Lemma 0.D.20 and obtain as a trivial consequence:

−ν∗​[F2​(θ)]+≤F1​(θ)−F∗+β​[F2​(θ)]+−β​[F2​(θ)]+.\displaystyle-{\nu^{*}}[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}\leq F_{1}({\theta})-{F^{*}}+\beta[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}-\beta[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}.

Taking expectation concludes the claim. ∎

Corollary 0.D.22 (Constraint Violation, Quadratic Penalty).

Assume that for (CME) strong duality holds with a Lagrangian multiplier ν∗≥0{\nu^{*}}\geq 0, and let θ∈Θ{\theta}\in{\Theta} be a point such that 𝔼⁡[P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ)]≤ε{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta})\right]\leq{\varepsilon} with the quadratic penalty. Then we have the following translation for the constraint violation:

𝔼⁡[[F2​(θ)]+]≤ν∗+ν∗2+2​β​εβ.\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}\right]\leq\frac{{\nu^{*}}+\sqrt{{\nu^{*}}^{2}+2\beta{\varepsilon}}}{\beta}.
Proof.

We invoke Lemma 0.D.20 and obtain

ε≥𝔼⁡[P2,β𝗈𝗉𝗍​(θ)]=𝔼⁡[F1​(θ)−F∗+β​[F2​(θ)]+2]​≥Jensen−ν∗​𝔼​[[F2​(θ)]+]+β​(𝔼⁡[[F2​(θ)]+])2.\displaystyle{\varepsilon}\geq{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[P^{\mathsf{opt}}_{2,\beta}({\theta})\right]={\mathbb{E}}\!\left[F_{1}({\theta})-{F^{*}}+\beta{[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}^{2}}\right]\overset{\text{Jensen}}{\geq}-{\nu^{*}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}\right]+\beta\left({\mathbb{E}}\!\left[[F_{2}({\theta})]_{+}\right]\right)^{2}.

Solving

s⁡(β⋅s−ν∗)−ε≤0,s.t.​s≥0\displaystyle s\left(\beta\cdot s-{\nu^{*}}\right)-{\varepsilon}\leq 0,\;\text{s.t.}\;s\geq 0

concludes the claim. ∎

Appendix 0.E Experimental Details & Ablation Studies

0.E.1 Grid World: Linear Performance Constraint

In this ablation study, we perform a Maximum Entropy exploration under a linear performance constraint, i.e. (CME) of the form

maxθ∈Θ\displaystyle\max_{\theta\in\Theta} ℋ⁡(λπθ)\displaystyle\;{\mathcal{H}}(\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}})
s.t. ⟨c,λπθ⟩≤0\displaystyle\;\langle c,\lambda^{\pi_{\theta}}\rangle\leq 0

where the cost function is of the form

c⁡(s)={50,s=Hole−0.001,else,\displaystyle c({s})=\begin{cases}50,&{s}=\texttt{Hole}\\ -0.001,&\text{else}\end{cases}, (ℛlin{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{lin}})

i.e. penalizing the four holes in the center of the environment Figure 5(a). We ablate the penalty parameter β∈{5⋅10−4,0.001,0.005,0.01}\beta\in\{5\cdot 10^{-4},0.001,0.005,0.01\}, the batch sizes B∈{8,24,72}B\in\{8,24,72\}, and the step sizes η∈{0.001,0.01,0.1}\eta\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1\}. We want to highlight that episodes terminate upon reaching the bottom-right tile. Consequently, the corresponding terminal state has an estimated occupancy λ^{\widehat{\lambda}} of almost zero for all methods, as it does not contribute informative state-action visitation beyond termination.

The full ablation results of the objective are shown in Figure 7, for the constraint in Figure 8 respectively.

Penalty Parameter β\beta.

Since our analysis requires β∼ε−1\beta\sim{\varepsilon}^{-1}, we validate empirically that this is actually not required in practice. While bigger β\beta might be indeed necessary to balance the tradeoff between improvement on the objective function and the constraint violation, cf. Figure 8, we ablate in Section 0.E.1.2 that the order of magnitude of β\beta rather depends on the scale of the safety constraint and does not necessarily have to be huge in practice. Checkpoint convergence results for both the grid world and SafeCartpole are reported in Table 1 in the main text.

Batch Size BB.

While the penalty parameter β\beta plays a significant role ensuring constraint violation, the batch size is elementary for the objective function. Larger BB becomes more important if one wants to increase the step size to speed-up the training process, cf. Figure 7. Empirically, we cannot observe that batches of B∼ε−4B\sim{\varepsilon}^{-4} are necessary, indicating that our estimates are most likely too conservative.

SGD Step Size η\eta.

The step size plays a crucial role, in particular to ensure convergence in the objective. In particular the interplay between the batch size BB and η\eta suggests, that both of them have to be chosen proportionally.

Implementation Details Primal-Dual [135].

We implement the primal-dual method of Ying et al. [135] as a baseline and perform a hyperparameter search for the primal and dual learning rate αθ,αμ\alpha_{\theta},\alpha_{\mu} and the momentum term αt\alpha_{t} in the notation of Ying et al. [135] Algorithm 1, for parameters αθ∈{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5,1}\alpha_{\theta}\in\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5,1\}, αμ∈{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5,1}\alpha_{\mu}\in\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5,1\}, and αt∈{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.03,0.05,0.1,1}\alpha_{t}\in\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.03,0.05,0.1,1\}. We also ablate the batch size B∈{8,24,72}B\in\{8,24,72\}, as for our PGP-method and pick the best configuration (αθ=0.01\alpha_{\theta}=0.01, αμ=0.001\alpha_{\mu}=0.001, α=1\alpha=1, i.e. no momentum) displayed in Figure 2. Interestingly, also for the primal-dual method, the batch size does not significantly change the performance, which is why we focus in Figure 2 on B=8B=8 for the sake of comparability. In our experiments, we could not see an improvement using their variance reduction momentum scheme: the resulting policies exhibited the oscillating constraint violation behavior and the best performance was achieved with αt≡1\alpha_{t}\equiv 1, t∈[T]t\in[T].

0.E.1.1 Unconstrained Baseline

For comparison, we also run the unconstrained baseline where we maximize entropy without any safety constraints. In particular, we run our penalty algorithm with β=0.0\beta=0.0 which corresponds to running unconstrained SGD to maximize the entropy and evaluate the constraint violation with respect to ( R lin ). The results are shown in Figure 6.

0.E.1.2 Lower Penalty for Holes, Increased β\beta required

As already suspected in Section 6.1, we find that choosing the penalty parameter β\beta does not have such a strong dependency on ∼ε−1\sim{\varepsilon}^{-1} but rather inversely proportionally depends on the scale of the cost function. To test this hypothesis, we modify the cost function ( R lin ) to a relaxed version with a −2-2 penalty for the Holes, i.e.

c⁡(s)={2,s=Hole−0.001,else,\displaystyle c({s})=\begin{cases}2,&{s}=\texttt{Hole}\\ -0.001,&\text{else}\end{cases}, (ℛlin,relax{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{lin},\mathrm{relax}})

as an alternative. As mentioned in the analysis of Section 5 in Section 6.1, we argue that the choice of β\beta in practice does not necessarily scale with ∼ε−1\sim{\varepsilon}^{-1}, but should be rather chosen depending on the scale of the reward, i.e. entropy maximization, and the order of magnitude of the constraint, in order to balance the constraint violation and the reward maximization. In particular, if we adjust the safety formulation to ( R lin , relax ), i.e. a lower penalty for acting unsafe, we require the penalty parameter β\beta to be larger to achieve similar results, as shown in Figure 10 and Figure 11, respectively, as we expected. Compared to the previous run, also in this case the step size η=0.1\eta=0.1 seems to be too big to either converge or deliver competitive results.

0.E.2 Grid World: Reference Trajectory Constraint – Norm Constraint

In order to showcase our method’s capability of performing maximum entropy exploration beyond linear constraints, we focus on a safe exploration task under imitation learning constraints. The reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is, in the notation of Figure 5(a), first going all the way to the right and then down until it terminates in the bottom right tile. We encode the constrained problem with an ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm constraint of the form

ℛℓ2​(λπ)≔∥λπ−λπref∥2≤b,\displaystyle{\mathcal{R}}_{\ell_{2}}(\lambda^{\pi})\coloneqq\lVert\lambda^{\pi}-\lambda^{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\rVert_{2}\leq b, (ℛℓ2{\mathcal{R}}_{\ell_{2}})

for a constraint violation budget b∈ℝ>0b\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}.

We ablate different values of b∈{0.0,0.2,0.5,1.0}b\in\{0.0,0.2,0.5,1.0\} and run our penalty method with β=0.5\beta=0.5 and a batch size of B=8B=8.

Results.

The final policies for each bb are visualized in Figure 12 and the corresponding training progress in Figure 13. One can clearly see that as the shift bb increases, the constraint becomes looser; thus the policy can deviate further from the reference policy and obtain a higher entropy value.

0.E.3 Continuous State-Action Space

We first discuss details on the estimation of the state-action occupancy measure and then provide details on the PointMass and the SafeCartpole experiment.

0.E.3.1 Occupancy Measure Estimate

When scaling to continuous state-action spaces in constrained maximum entropy exploration, or more generally in convex RL, reliably estimating the occupancy measure ( λ MC H -Est) is the main bottleneck. In our case, we use and implement the state-of-the-art technique proposed by Barakat et al. [12] relying on Maximum Likelihood Estimators (MLE) for learning the approximation λ^{\widehat{\lambda}} compared to the Mean Squared Error, which previous techniques have been proposing. Compared to our formulation of λπ:𝒮×𝒜→[0,1]\lambda^{\pi}:{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to[0,1] as a function of the state and action space, Barakat et al. [12] rewrite λπ\lambda^{\pi} of a policy π\pi in the form

λπ​(s,a)≔dπ​(s)⋅π⁡(a|s),\displaystyle\lambda^{\pi}({s},{a})\coloneqq d^{\pi}({s})\cdot\pi({a}|{s}),

and only approximate the state-occupancy measure dπd^{\pi} with a function approximator.

In particular, at every step of the algorithm, we collect a batch of Nλ^∈ℕN_{{\widehat{\lambda}}}\in{\mathbb{N}} samples Bλ^≔{si,ai}i∈[Nλ^]B_{{\widehat{\lambda}}}\coloneqq\{{s}_{i},{a}_{i}\}_{i\in[N_{{\widehat{\lambda}}}]}, consisting of potentially several rollouts and then approximate dπd^{\pi} with a parametric class of probability distributions

GMM(K)≔{pw≔∑k=1Kwk𝒩(𝐦k,Σk):w=(wk,𝐦k,Σk)k∈[K]\displaystyle\mathrm{GMM}(K)\coloneqq\left\{p_{\textbf{w}}\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}_{k},\Sigma_{k}):{\textbf{w}}=(w_{k},\mathbf{m}_{k},\Sigma_{k})_{k\in[K]}\right.
s.t.wk≥0,∑k=1Kwk=1,𝐦k∈ℝds,Σk∈𝕊+⁣+ds,}\displaystyle\left.\;\mathrm{s.t.}\;w_{k}\geq 0,\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}=1,\mathbf{m}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}},\Sigma_{k}\in\mathbb{S}^{d_{s}}_{++},\right\}

in our case Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), with K=16K=16. The approximation d^π\hat{d}^{\pi} is learned by maximizing the MLE loss, or equivalently minimizing a Kullback Leibler divergence [108], i.e.

d^π≔pw∗,pw∗∈arg​maxpw∈GMM⁡(K)⁡1Nλ^​∑i∈[Nλ^]log⁡pw​(si).\displaystyle\hat{d}^{\pi}\coloneqq p_{{\textbf{w}}^{*}},\quad p_{{\textbf{w}}^{*}}\in\argmax_{p_{\textbf{w}}\in\mathrm{GMM}(K)}\frac{1}{N_{{\widehat{\lambda}}}}\sum_{i\in[N_{{\widehat{\lambda}}}]}\log p_{\textbf{w}}({s}_{i}). (d^π\hat{d}^{\pi}-Est)

Following Barakat et al. [12], the estimate λ^π{\widehat{\lambda}}^{\pi} is then given by

λ^π​(s,a)≔d^π​(s)⋅π⁡(a|s).\displaystyle{\widehat{\lambda}}^{\pi}({s},{a})\coloneqq\hat{d}^{\pi}({s})\cdot\pi({a}|{s}). (λHMLE\lambda^{\mathrm{MLE}}_{H}-Est)

0.E.3.2 Imitation Learning Constraint: PointMass Exploration

We provide additional implementation and computational details on the PointMass experiment.

State, Action & Observation Space.

In the PointMass environment, the state, action and observation space are

𝒮×𝒜×Obs=ℝ2×ℝ2×ℝ2.\displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\times\Obs={\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.

At timestep tt, each observation oto_{t} consists of the current xx and yy coordinate of the point mass. The action a{a} encodes the gain along the xx and yy-axis respectively.

Objective and Constraint: Definition & Implementation.

First, we train a reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} using the Soft-Actor critic (SAC) algorithm of the StableBaselines3 package [101]. We fit the reference GMM from stochastic SAC rollouts using the same discounted weighted likelihood as in ( ^ d π -Est). On a batch BB, the apprenticeship constraint and its pseudo-reward are

ℛ^KL\displaystyle\widehat{{\mathcal{R}}}_{\rm KL} ≔∑i∈Bw¯i​(log⁡λ^π​(si,ai)−log⁡λ^ref​(si,ai))−ℛmax,\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{i\in B}\bar{w}_{i}\left(\log{\widehat{\lambda}}^{\pi}({s}_{i},{a}_{i})-\log{\widehat{\lambda}}^{\rm ref}({s}_{i},{a}_{i})\right)-{\mathcal{R}_{\max}},
rKL​(si,ai)\displaystyle r_{\rm KL}({s}_{i},{a}_{i}) ≔1+log⁡λ^π​(si,ai)−log⁡λ^ref​(si,ai).\displaystyle\coloneqq 1+\log{\widehat{\lambda}}^{\pi}({s}_{i},{a}_{i})-\log{\widehat{\lambda}}^{\rm ref}({s}_{i},{a}_{i}).

The budget ℛmax{\mathcal{R}_{\max}} affects the constraint value but, being constant, does not enter its pseudo-reward.

Analysis of Actions.

Figure 14 shows that as the constraint budget ℛmax{\mathcal{R}_{\max}} increases, the actions of πθ\pi_{\theta} deviate progressively further from those of πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. This directly reflects the difficulty of the task: the SAC reference policy consistently directs the agent toward the goal (0,0)(0,0), so effective exploration requires substantial deviation from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}.

0.E.3.3 Safety Constrained: Cartpole Exploration

We provide implementation and computational details on the SafeCartpole experiment.

State, Action & Observation Space.

In the SafeCartpole environment, the state, action and observation space are

𝒮×𝒜×Obs=ℝ4×ℝ×ℝ5,\displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\times\Obs={\mathbb{R}}^{4}\times{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{5}, (15)

where each observation oto_{t} at timestep t∈[0,Tmax]t\in[0,{T_{\max}}] consists of

ot=[xt,sin⁡(ωt),cos⁡(ωt),dd​t​xt,dd​t​ωt]∈ℝ5,\displaystyle o_{t}=[x_{t},\sin(\omega_{t}),\cos(\omega_{t}),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\>\mathrm{d}t}x_{t},\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\>\mathrm{d}t}\omega_{t}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{5}, (oto_{t}-Cartpole)

and ωt\omega_{t} is the current angle of the pole, xtx_{t} the slider’s position with its corresponding velocity, and the last component encodes the angular velocity of the pole via the corresponding time derivatives of the angular observations. The state consists of

st=[xt,dd​t​xt,ωt,dd​t​ωt]∈ℝ4,\displaystyle{s}_{t}=[x_{t},\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\>\mathrm{d}t}x_{t},\omega_{t},\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\>\mathrm{d}t}\omega_{t}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{4},

i.e. includes not only the position and the angle, but also their corresponding derivatives. Thus, effective exploration of the state action space requires covering the position and velocity of the cart as well as the angles of the pole, and also entails the angular velocities of the pole, making the task significantly harder for constrained maximum entropy. An action at∈ℝ{a}_{t}\in{\mathbb{R}} is a real-valued action which is passed through a motor gear and then acts on the system.

Objective and Constraint: Definition & Implementation Details.

After the state-action occupancy measure is estimated via the MLE in ( ^ d π -Est), we can estimate the entropy objective and the constraint.

The constraint function is given by

c⁡(st,at)≔max⁡(|xt|−2.0,0),\displaystyle c({s}_{t},{a}_{t})\coloneqq\max(\lvert x_{t}\rvert-2.0,0),

where xtx_{t} encodes the slider’s position at time t∈[0,Tmax]t\in[0,{T_{\max}}]. For the sake of presentation, we also log the values |xt|−2.0\lvert x_{t}\rvert-2.0 to make the constraint violation plot more expressive. The entropy and the cost function can be then computed by point-wise multiplications of the tensors given by: λ^{\widehat{\lambda}} evaluated on the state and action pairs, the logarithm of λ^{\widehat{\lambda}} for the objective and the constraint function values (c⁡(st,at))t(c({s}_{t},{a}_{t}))_{t} for each rollout, respectively. For numerical stability, we perform a log-sum-exp rescaling for these tensor computations. Afterwards we apply the squared penalty, sum both terms and obtain the pseudo-reward for which we compute the gradient using PyTorch’s [98] automatic differentiation framework. The resulting gradient is plugged in the (PG-Thm) to compute the cumulative reward and optimize. We use a critic network as a baseline for the REINFORCE algorithm to improve stability, i.e. (PG-Thm) acts on the advantage function.

Detailed Analysis of the Results.

We analyze separately:

  • •

    Entropy and Constraint Violation. In Figure 4(a) we observe a significant jump at N=1000N=1000 in the entropy ℋ{\mathcal{H}} which, combined with Figure 17 and additional logging information, corresponds to the policy understanding that symmetric discovery drastically improves the exploration in the state-action space. Afterwards, we observe a slight drop in the entropy again, as the policy needs to relearn, or more precisely combine, to turn the pole upwards and discover the space in a symmetric way. As evident in Figure 16 (bottom left), later episodes then learn how to push the penalty function right below the threshold to accelerate faster, i.e. get up the pole quicker and then discover even more. The final policy has almost perfect symmetry over the rollout horizon with varying angular velocities in the lower half of the angular part of the state space.

  • •

    Controls. Figure 16 shows that in particular early controls are slightly fuzzy and exhibit high(er) variance. In later iterations, i.e. k∈[1000,2500]∩ℕk\in[1000,2500]\cap{\mathbb{N}}, the policy π(k)\pi^{(k)} correctly learns a bang-bang control style, which is optimal to turn the pole upward, especially since we do not penalize actions in our setting. This behavior is for larger kk refined and the final policy perfectly flips the pole to the upper half of the angular’s state space and is confirmed as the correct behavior by the reduced variance σθ2\sigma^{2}_{\theta}, as it also improves on the tiny constraint violation at the end of the observation horizon.
